L2: Amazon SageMaker AI metrics in Amazon CloudWatch - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Endpoint metrics cite2†Endpoint invocation metrics cite3†Inference component metrics cite4†Multi-model endpoint metrics cite5†Job metrics cite6†Inference Recommender metrics cite7†Ground Truth metrics cite8†Feature Store metrics cite9†Pipelines metrics L5: # Amazon SageMaker AI metrics in Amazon CloudWatch
L6: You can monitor Amazon SageMaker AI using Amazon CloudWatch, which collects raw data and processes it into readable, near real-time metrics. These statistics are kept for 15 months. With them, you can access historical information and gain a better perspective on how your web application or service is performing. However, the Amazon CloudWatch console limits the search to metrics that were updated in the last 2 weeks. This limitation ensures that the most current jobs are shown in your namespace.
L7: To graph metrics without using a search, specify its exact name in the source view. You can also set alarms that watch for certain thresholds, and send notifications or take actions when those thresholds are met. For more information, see the cite10†Amazon CloudWatch User Guide .
L8: ###### SageMaker AI Metrics and Dimensions
L9: 
L10:   * cite1†SageMaker AI endpoint metrics L11: 
L12:   * cite2†SageMaker AI endpoint invocation metrics L13: 
L14:   * cite3†SageMaker AI inference component metrics L15: 
L16:   * cite4†SageMaker AI multi-model endpoint metrics L17: 
L18:   * cite5†SageMaker AI job metrics L19: 
L20:   * cite6†SageMaker Inference Recommender jobs metrics L21: 
L22:   * cite7†SageMaker Ground Truth metrics L23: 
L24:   * cite8†Amazon SageMaker Feature Store metrics L25: 
L26:   * cite9†SageMaker pipelines metrics L27: ## SageMaker AI endpoint metrics
L28: 
L29: The `/aws/sagemaker/Endpoints` namespace includes the following metrics for endpoint instances.
L30: Metrics are available at a 1-minute frequency. You can configure the publishing frequency to 10, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240, or 300 seconds by setting `MetricPublishFrequencyInSeconds` in cite11†MetricsConfig . This setting does not require `EnableEnhancedMetrics` to be enabled. When you set `EnableEnhancedMetrics` to `True`, the additional dimensions `InstanceId` and `AcceleratorId` (GPU metrics only) are available. For more information, see cite12†Amazon SageMaker AI enhanced metrics for inference endpoints .
L31: ###### Note
L32: 
L33: Amazon CloudWatch supports cite13†high-resolution custom metrics and its finest resolution is 1 second. However, the finer the resolution, the shorter the lifespan of the CloudWatch metrics. For the 1-second frequency resolution, the CloudWatch metrics are available for 3 hours. For more information about the resolution and the lifespan of the CloudWatch metrics, see cite14†GetMetricStatistics in the Amazon CloudWatch API Reference.
L34: Endpoint metrics
L35: Metric  | Description
L36: --- | ---
L37: `CPUReservation`  | The sum of CPUs reserved by containers on an instance. This metric is provided only for endpoints that host active inference components. The value ranges between 0%–100%. In the settings for an inference component, you set the CPU reservation with the `NumberOfCpuCoresRequired` parameter. For example, if there 4 CPUs, and 2 are reserved, the `CPUReservation` metric is 50%.
L38: `CPUUtilization`  | The sum of each individual CPU core's utilization. The CPU utilization of each core range is 0–100. For example, if there are four CPUs, the `CPUUtilization` range is 0%–400%. For endpoint variants, the value is the sum of the CPU utilization of the primary and supplementary containers on the instance. Units: Percent
L39: `CPUUtilizationNormalized`  | The normalized sum of the utilization of each individual CPU core. This metric is provided only for endpoints that host active inference components. The value ranges between 0%–100%. For example, if there are four CPUs, and the `CPUUtilization` metric is 200%, then the `CPUUtilizationNormalized` metric is 50%.
L40: `DiskUtilization`  | The percentage of disk space used by the containers on an instance. This value range is 0%–100%.For endpoint variants, the value is the sum of the disk space utilization of the primary and supplementary containers on the instance.Units: Percent
L41: `GPUMemoryUtilization`  | The percentage of GPU memory used by the containers on an instance. The value range is 0–100 and is multiplied by the number of GPUs. For example, if there are four GPUs, the `GPUMemoryUtilization` range is 0%–400%. For endpoint variants, the value is the sum of the GPU memory utilization of the primary and supplementary containers on the instance. Units: Percent
L42: `GPUMemoryUtilizationNormalized`  | The normalized percentage of GPU memory used by the containers on an instance. This metric is provided only for endpoints that host active inference components. The value ranges between 0%–100%. For example, if there are four GPUs, and the `GPUMemoryUtilization` metric is 200%, then the `GPUMemoryUtilizationNormalized` metric is 50%.
L43: `GPUReservation`  | The sum of GPUs reserved by containers on an instance. This metric is provided only for endpoints that host active inference components. The value ranges between 0%–100%. In the settings for an inference component, you set the GPU reservation by `NumberOfAcceleratorDevicesRequired`. For example, if there are 4 GPUs and 2 are reserved, the `GPUReservation` metric is 50%.
L44: `GPUUtilization`  | The percentage of GPU units that are used by the containers on an instance. The value can range between 0–100 and is multiplied by the number of GPUs. For example, if there are four GPUs, the `GPUUtilization` range is 0%–400%. For endpoint variants, the value is the sum of the GPU utilization of the primary and supplementary containers on the instance. Units: Percent
L45: `GPUUtilizationNormalized`  | The normalized percentage of GPU units that are used by the containers on an instance. This metric is provided only for endpoints that host active inference components. The value ranges between 0%–100%. For example, if there are four GPUs, and the `GPUUtilization` metric is 200%, then the `GPUUtilizationNormalized` metric is 50%.
L46: `MemoryReservation`  | The sum of memory reserved by containers on an instance. This metric is provided only for endpoints that host active inference components. The value ranges between 0%–100%. In the settings for an inference component, you set the memory reservation with the `MinMemoryRequiredInMb` parameter. For example, if a 32 GiB instance reserved 1024 MB, the `MemoryReservation` metric would be 3.125%.
L47: `MemoryUtilization`  | The percentage of memory that is used by the containers on an instance. This value range is 0%–100%. For endpoint variants, the value is the sum of the memory utilization of the primary and supplementary containers on the instance. Units: Percent
L48: Dimensions for endpoint metrics
L49: Dimension  | Description
L50: --- | ---
L51: `EndpointName, VariantName`  | Filters endpoint metrics for a `ProductionVariant` of the specified endpoint and variant.
L52: `EndpointName, VariantName, InstanceType`  | Filters endpoint metrics by instance type for a production variant that uses instance pools. Use this dimension to monitor metrics for each instance type within the variant separately.
L53: `InstanceId`  | Filters endpoint metrics for a specific instance. Available when `EnableEnhancedMetrics` is set to `True` in `MetricsConfig`.
L54: `AcceleratorId`  | (GPU metrics only) Filters endpoint metrics for a specific GPU. Available when `EnableEnhancedMetrics` is set to `True` in `MetricsConfig`.
L55: ## SageMaker AI endpoint invocation metrics
L56: 
L57: The `AWS/SageMaker` namespace includes the following request metrics from calls to cite15†InvokeEndpoint .
L58: Metrics are available at a 1-minute frequency. You can configure the publishing frequency to 10, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240, or 300 seconds by setting `MetricPublishFrequencyInSeconds` in cite11†MetricsConfig . For invocation metrics, this setting requires `EnableEnhancedMetrics` to be set to `True`. When you set `EnableEnhancedMetrics` to `True`, the additional dimensions `InstanceId` and `ContainerId` (inference components only) are also available.
L59: For more information, see cite12†Amazon SageMaker AI enhanced metrics for inference endpoints .
L60: The following illustration shows how a SageMaker AI endpoint interacts with the Amazon SageMaker Runtime API. The overall time between sending a request to an endpoint and receiving a response depends on the following three components.
L61: 
L62:   * Network latency – the time that it takes between making a request to and receiving a response back from the SageMaker Runtime Runtime API.
L63:   * Overhead latency – the time that it takes to transport a request to the model container from and transport the response back to the SageMaker Runtime Runtime API.
L64: 
L65:   * Model latency – the time that it takes the model container to process the request and return a response.
L66: 
L67: cite16†Image: An illustration showing that total latency is the sum of network, overhead and model latencies. L68: For more information about total latency, see cite17†Best practices for load testing Amazon SageMaker AI real-time inference endpoints†aws.amazon.com . For information about how long CloudWatch metrics are retained for, see cite14†GetMetricStatistics in the Amazon CloudWatch API Reference.
L69: Endpoint invocation metrics
L70: Metric  | Description
L71: --- | ---
L72: `ConcurrentRequestsPerCopy`  | The number of concurrent requests being received by the inference component, normalized by each copy of an inference component. Valid statistics: Min, Max
L73: `ConcurrentRequestsPerModel`  | The number of concurrent requests being received by the model. Valid statistics: Min, Max
L74: `Invocation4XXErrors`  | The number of `InvokeEndpoint` requests where the model returned a 4xx HTTP response code. For each 4xx response, 1 is sent; otherwise, 0 is sent. Units: None Valid statistics: Average, Sum
L75: `Invocation5XXErrors`  | The number of `InvokeEndpoint` requests where the model returned a 5xx HTTP response code. For each 5xx response, 1 is sent; otherwise, 0 is sent. Units: None Valid statistics: Average, Sum
L76: `InvocationModelErrors`  | The number of model invocation requests that did not result in 2XX HTTP response. This includes 4XX/5XX status codes, low-level socket errors, malformed HTTP responses, and request timeouts. For each error response, 1 is sent; otherwise, 0 is sent. Units: None Valid statistics: Average, Sum
L77: `Invocations`  | The number of `InvokeEndpoint` requests sent to a model endpoint. To get the total number of requests sent to a model endpoint, use the Sum statistic. Units: None Valid statistics: Sum
L78: `InvocationsPerCopy`  | The number of invocations normalized by each copy of an inference component. Valid statistics: Sum
L79: `InvocationsPerInstance`  | The number of invocations sent to a model, normalized by `InstanceCount` in each ProductionVariant. 1/`numberOfInstances` is sent as the value on each request. `numberOfInstances` is the number of active instances for the ProductionVariant behind the endpoint at the time of the request. Units: None Valid statistics: Sum
L80: `ModelLatency`  | The interval of time taken by a model to respond to a SageMaker Runtime API request. This interval includes the local communication times taken to send the request and to fetch the response from the model container. It also includes the time taken to complete the inference in the container. Units: Microseconds Valid statistics: Average, Sum, Min, Max, Sample Count, Percentiles
L81: `ModelSetupTime`  | The time it takes to launch new compute resources for a serverless endpoint. The time can vary depending on the model size, how long it takes to download the model, and the start-up time of the container. Units: Microseconds Valid statistics: Average, Min, Max, Sample Count, Percentiles
L82: `OverheadLatency`  | The interval of time added to the time taken to respond to a client request by SageMaker AI overheads. This interval is measured from the time SageMaker AI receives the request until it returns a response to the client, minus the `ModelLatency`. Overhead latency can vary depending on multiple factors, including request and response payload sizes, request frequency, and authentication/authorization of the request.
L83: Units: Microseconds Valid statistics: Average, Sum, Min, Max, Sample Count
L84: `MidStreamErrors`  | The number of errors that occur during response streaming after the initial response has been sent to the customer. Units: None Valid statistics: Average, Sum

L6: Linear models are supervised learning algorithms used for solving either classification or regression problems. For input, you give the model labeled examples (x, y). x is a high-dimensional vector and y is a numeric label. For binary classification problems, the label must be either 0 or 1. For multiclass classification problems, the labels must be from 0 to `num_classes` - 1. For regression problems, y is a real number.
L7: The algorithm learns a linear function, or, for classification problems, a linear threshold function, and maps a vector x to an approximation of the label y.
L8: The Amazon SageMaker AI linear learner algorithm provides a solution for both classification and regression problems. With the SageMaker AI algorithm, you can simultaneously explore different training objectives and choose the best solution from a validation set. You can also explore a large number of models and choose the best. The best model optimizes either of the following:
L9: 
L10:   * Continuous objectives, such as mean square error, cross entropy loss, absolute error.
L11:   * Discrete objectives suited for classification, such as F1 measure, precision, recall, or accuracy.
L12: 
L13: Compared with methods that provide a solution for only continuous objectives, the SageMaker AI linear learner algorithm provides a significant increase in speed over naive hyperparameter optimization techniques. It is also more convenient.
L14: The linear learner algorithm requires a data matrix, with rows representing the observations, and columns representing the dimensions of the features. It also requires an additional column that contains the labels that match the data points. At a minimum, Amazon SageMaker AI linear learner requires you to specify input and output data locations, and objective type (classification or regression) as arguments. The feature dimension is also required. For more information, see cite4†`CreateTrainingJob` .
L15: You can specify additional parameters in the `HyperParameters` string map of the request body. These parameters control the optimization procedure, or specifics of the objective function that you train on. For example, the number of epochs, regularization, and loss type.
L16: If you're using cite5†Managed Spot Training , the linear learner algorithm supports using cite6†checkpoints to take a snapshot of the state of the model .

L31:   * cite10†Linear learner response formats L32: ## Input/Output interface for the linear learner algorithm
L33: The Amazon SageMaker AI linear learner algorithm supports three data channels: train, validation (optional), and test (optional). If you provide validation data, the `S3DataDistributionType` should be `FullyReplicated`. The algorithm logs validation loss at every epoch, and uses a sample of the validation data to calibrate and select the best model. If you don't provide validation data, the algorithm uses a sample of the training data to calibrate and select the model.
L34: If you provide test data, the algorithm logs include the test score for the final model.
L35: For training, the linear learner algorithm supports both `recordIO-wrapped protobuf` and `CSV` formats. For the `application/x-recordio-protobuf` input type, only Float32 tensors are supported. For the `text/csv` input type, the first column is assumed to be the label, which is the target variable for prediction. You can use either File mode or Pipe mode to train linear learner models on data that is formatted as `recordIO-wrapped-protobuf` or as `CSV`.
L36: For inference, the linear learner algorithm supports the `application/json`, `application/x-recordio-protobuf`, and `text/csv` formats. When you make predictions on new data, the format of the response depends on the type of model. For regression (`predictor_type='regressor'`), the `score` is the prediction produced by the model. For classification (`predictor_type='binary_classifier'` or `predictor_type='multiclass_classifier'`), the model returns a `score` and also a `predicted_label`.
L37: The `predicted_label` is the class predicted by the model and the `score` measures the strength of that prediction.
L38:   * For binary classification, `predicted_label` is `0` or `1`, and `score` is a single floating point number that indicates how strongly the algorithm believes that the label should be 1.
L39: 
L40:   * For multiclass classification, the `predicted_class` will be an integer from `0` to `num_classes-1`, and `score` will be a list of one floating point number per class.
L41: To interpret the `score` in classification problems, you have to consider the loss function used. If the `loss` hyperparameter value is `logistic` for binary classification or `softmax_loss` for multiclass classification, then the `score` can be interpreted as the probability of the corresponding class. These are the loss values used by the linear learner when the `loss` value is `auto` default value. But if the loss is set to `hinge_loss`, then the score cannot be interpreted as a probability.
L42: This is because hinge loss corresponds to a Support Vector Classifier, which does not produce probability estimates.
L43: For more information on input and output file formats, see cite10†Linear learner response formats . For more information on inference formats, and the cite3†Linear learner sample notebooks .
L44: ## EC2 instance recommendation for the linear learner algorithm
L45: 
L46: The linear learner algorithm supports both CPU and GPU instances for training and inference. For GPU, the linear learner algorithm supports P2, P3, G4dn, and G5 GPU families.
L47: 
L48: During testing, we have not found substantial evidence that multi-GPU instances are faster than single-GPU instances. Results can vary, depending on your specific use case.

citeturn41view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 6 days ago; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/object2vec.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 85
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: Object2Vec Algorithm - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†I/O Interface for the Object2Vec Algorithm cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the Object2Vec Algorithm cite3†Sample Notebooks L5: # Object2Vec Algorithm
L6: The Amazon SageMaker AI Object2Vec algorithm is a general-purpose neural embedding algorithm that is highly customizable. It can learn low-dimensional dense embeddings of high-dimensional objects. The embeddings are learned in a way that preserves the semantics of the relationship between pairs of objects in the original space in the embedding space.
L7: You can use the learned embeddings to efficiently compute nearest neighbors of objects and to visualize natural clusters of related objects in low-dimensional space, for example. You can also use the embeddings as features of the corresponding objects in downstream supervised tasks, such as classification or regression.
L8: Object2Vec generalizes the well-known Word2Vec embedding technique for words that is optimized in the SageMaker AI cite4†BlazingText algorithm . For a blog post that discusses how to apply Object2Vec to some practical use cases, see cite5†Introduction to Amazon SageMaker AI Object2Vec†aws.amazon.com .
L9: ###### Topics
L10:

L25:   * cite10†Data Formats for Object2Vec Inference L26: 
L27:   * cite11†Encoder Embeddings for Object2Vec L28: ## I/O Interface for the Object2Vec Algorithm
L29: 
L30: You can use Object2Vec on many input data types, including the following examples.
L31: Input Data Type  | Example
L32: --- | ---
L33: Sentence-sentence pairs  | "A soccer game with multiple males playing." and "Some men are playing a sport."
L34: Labels-sequence pairs  | The genre tags of the movie "Titanic", such as "Romance" and "Drama", and its short description: "James Cameron's Titanic is an epic, action-packed romance set against the ill-fated maiden voyage of the R.M.S. Titanic. She was the most luxurious liner of her era, a ship of dreams, which ultimately carried over 1,500 people to their death in the ice cold waters of the North Atlantic in the early hours of April 15, 1912."
L35: Customer-customer pairs  | The customer ID of Jane and customer ID of Jackie.
L36: Product-product pairs  | The product ID of football and product ID of basketball.
L37: Item review user-item pairs  | A user's ID and the items she has bought, such as apple, pear, and orange.
L38: To transform the input data into the supported formats, you must preprocess it. Currently, Object2Vec natively supports two types of input:
L39: 
L40:   * A discrete token, which is represented as a list of a single `integer-id`. For example, `[10]`.
L41: 
L42:   * A sequences of discrete tokens, which is represented as a list of `integer-ids`. For example, `[0,12,10,13]`.
L43: The object in each pair can be asymmetric. For example, the pairs can be (token, sequence) or (token, token) or (sequence, sequence). For token inputs, the algorithm supports simple embeddings as compatible encoders. For sequences of token vectors, the algorithm supports the following as encoders:
L44: 
L45:   * Average-pooled embeddings
L46: 
L47:   * Hierarchical convolutional neural networks (CNNs),
L48: 
L49:   * Multi-layered bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTMs)
L50: The input label for each pair can be one of the following:
L51: 
L52:   * A categorical label that expresses the relationship between the objects in the pair
L53: 
L54:   * A score that expresses the strength of the similarity between the two objects
L55: For categorical labels used in classification, the algorithm supports the cross-entropy loss function. For ratings/score-based labels used in regression, the algorithm supports the mean squared error (MSE) loss function. Specify these loss functions with the `output_layer` hyperparameter when you create the model training job.
L56: ## EC2 Instance Recommendation for the Object2Vec Algorithm
L57: 
L58: The type of Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance that you use depends on whether you are training or running inference.
L59: When training a model using the Object2Vec algorithm on a CPU, start with an ml.m5.2xlarge instance. For training on a GPU, start with an ml.p2.xlarge instance. If the training takes too long on this instance, you can use a larger instance. Currently, the Object2Vec algorithm can train only on a single machine. However, it does offer support for multiple GPUs. Object2Vec supports P2, P3, G4dn, and G5 GPU instance families for training and inference.
L60: For inference with a trained Object2Vec model that has a deep neural network, we recommend using ml.p3.2xlarge GPU instance. Due to GPU memory scarcity, the `INFERENCE_PREFERRED_MODE` environment variable can be specified to optimize on whether the cite12†GPU optimization: Classification or Regression or cite13†GPU optimization: Encoder Embeddings inference network is loaded into GPU.

L6: 
L7: Starts a model training job. After training completes, SageMaker saves the resulting model artifacts to an Amazon S3 location that you specify.
L8: 
L9: If you choose to host your model using SageMaker hosting services, you can use the resulting model artifacts as part of the model. You can also use the artifacts in a machine learning service other than SageMaker, provided that you know how to use them for inference.
L10: 
L11: In the request body, you provide the following:
L12:   * `AlgorithmSpecification` - Identifies the training algorithm to use.
L13: 
L14:   * `HyperParameters` - Specify these algorithm-specific parameters to enable the estimation of model parameters during training. Hyperparameters can be tuned to optimize this learning process. For a list of hyperparameters for each training algorithm provided by SageMaker, see cite7†Algorithms .
L15: ###### Important
L16: 
L17: Do not include any security-sensitive information including account access IDs, secrets, or tokens in any hyperparameter fields. As part of the shared responsibility model, you are responsible for any potential exposure, unauthorized access, or compromise of your sensitive data if caused by security-sensitive information included in the request hyperparameter variable or plain text fields.
L18:   * `InputDataConfig` - Describes the input required by the training job and the Amazon S3, EFS, or FSx location where it is stored.
L19: 
L20:   * `OutputDataConfig` - Identifies the Amazon S3 bucket where you want SageMaker to save the results of model training.
L21: 
L22:   * `ResourceConfig` - Identifies the resources, ML compute instances, and ML storage volumes to deploy for model training. In distributed training, you specify more than one instance.
L23:   * `EnableManagedSpotTraining` - Optimize the cost of training machine learning models by up to 80% by using Amazon EC2 Spot instances. For more information, see cite8†Managed Spot Training .
L24: 
L25:   * `RoleArn` - The Amazon Resource Name (ARN) that SageMaker assumes to perform tasks on your behalf during model training. You must grant this role the necessary permissions so that SageMaker can successfully complete model training.
L26:   * `StoppingCondition` - To help cap training costs, use `MaxRuntimeInSeconds` to set a time limit for training. Use `MaxWaitTimeInSeconds` to specify how long a managed spot training job has to complete.
L27: 
L28:   * `Environment` - The environment variables to set in the Docker container.
L29: ###### Important
L30: 
L31: Do not include any security-sensitive information including account access IDs, secrets, or tokens in any environment fields. As part of the shared responsibility model, you are responsible for any potential exposure, unauthorized access, or compromise of your sensitive data if caused by security-sensitive information included in the request environment variable or plain text fields.
L32:   * `RetryStrategy` - The number of times to retry the job when the job fails due to an `InternalServerError`.
L33: 
L34: For more information about SageMaker, see cite9†How It Works .

BlazingText algorithm - Amazon SageMaker AI (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/blazingtext.html)
citeturn43view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/blazingtext.html","lineno":null}); Total lines: 173
L0: cite0†View a markdown version of this page L1: 
L2: BlazingText algorithm - Amazon SageMaker AI
L3: 
L4: cite1†Input/Output Interface for the BlazingText Algorithm cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the BlazingText Algorithm cite3†Sample Notebooks L5: # BlazingText algorithm
L6: 
L7: The Amazon SageMaker AI BlazingText algorithm provides highly optimized implementations of the Word2vec and text classification algorithms. The Word2vec algorithm is useful for many downstream natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, machine translation, etc. Text classification is an important task for applications that perform web searches, information retrieval, ranking, and document classification.
L8: The Word2vec algorithm maps words to high-quality distributed vectors. The resulting vector representation of a word is called a word embedding. Words that are semantically similar correspond to vectors that are close together. That way, word embeddings capture the semantic relationships between words.
L9: Many natural language processing (NLP) applications learn word embeddings by training on large collections of documents. These pretrained vector representations provide information about semantics and word distributions that typically improves the generalizability of other models that are later trained on a more limited amount of data. Most implementations of the Word2vec algorithm are not optimized for multi-core CPU architectures. This makes it difficult to scale to large datasets.
L10: With the BlazingText algorithm, you can scale to large datasets easily. Similar to Word2vec, it provides the Skip-gram and continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) training architectures. BlazingText's implementation of the supervised multi-class, multi-label text classification algorithm extends the fastText text classifier to use GPU acceleration with custom cite4†CUDA†docs.nvidia.com kernels. You can train a model on more than a billion words in a couple of minutes using a multi-core CPU or a GPU.
L11: And, you achieve performance on par with the state-of-the-art deep learning text classification algorithms.
L12: The BlazingText algorithm is not parallelizable. For more information on parameters related to training, see cite5†Docker Registry Paths for SageMaker Built-in Algorithms .
L13: 
L14: The SageMaker AI BlazingText algorithms provides the following features:
L15: 
L16:   * Accelerated training of the fastText text classifier on multi-core CPUs or a GPU and Word2Vec on GPUs using highly optimized CUDA kernels. For more information, see cite6†BlazingText: Scaling and Accelerating Word2Vec using Multiple GPUs†dl.acm.org .
L17:   * cite7†Enriched Word Vectors with Subword Information†arxiv.org by learning vector representations for character n-grams. This approach enables BlazingText to generate meaningful vectors for out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words by representing their vectors as the sum of the character n-gram (subword) vectors.
L18:   * A `batch_skipgram` `mode` for the Word2Vec algorithm that allows faster training and distributed computation across multiple CPU nodes. The `batch_skipgram` `mode` does mini-batching using the Negative Sample Sharing strategy to convert level-1 BLAS operations into level-3 BLAS operations. This efficiently leverages the multiply-add instructions of modern architectures. For more information, see cite8†Parallelizing Word2Vec in Shared and Distributed Memory†arxiv.org .
L19: To summarize, the following modes are supported by BlazingText on different types instances:
L20: 
L21: Modes  | Word2Vec (Unsupervised Learning)  | Text Classification (Supervised Learning)
L22: --- | --- | ---
L23: Single CPU instance  | `cbow` `Skip-gram` `Batch Skip-gram`  | `supervised`
L24: Single GPU instance (with 1 or more GPUs)  | `cbow` `Skip-gram`  | `supervised` with one GPU
L25: Multiple CPU instances  | `Batch Skip-gram `  | None
L26: For more information about the mathematics behind BlazingText, see cite6†BlazingText: Scaling and Accelerating Word2Vec using Multiple GPUs†dl.acm.org .
L27: ###### Topics
L28: 
L29:   * cite1†Input/Output Interface for the BlazingText Algorithm L30: 
L31:   * cite2†EC2 Instance Recommendation for the BlazingText Algorithm L32: 
L33:   * cite3†BlazingText Sample Notebooks L34: 
L35:   * cite9†BlazingText Hyperparameters L36: 
L37:   * cite10†Tune a BlazingText Model L38: ## Input/Output Interface for the BlazingText Algorithm
L39: 
L40: The BlazingText algorithm expects a single preprocessed text file with space-separated tokens. Each line in the file should contain a single sentence. If you need to train on multiple text files, concatenate them into one file and upload the file in the respective channel.
L41: 
L42: ### Training and Validation Data Format
L43: #### Training and Validation Data Format for the Word2Vec Algorithm
L44: 
L45: For Word2Vec training, upload the file under the train channel. No other channels are supported. The file should contain a training sentence per line.
L46: 
L47: #### Training and Validation Data Format for the Text Classification Algorithm
L48: 
L49: For supervised mode, you can train with file mode or with the augmented manifest text format.
L50: ##### Train with File Mode
L51: For `supervised` mode, the training/validation file should contain a training sentence per line along with the labels. Labels are words that are prefixed by the string __label__. Here is an example of a training/validation file:
L52: 
L53:     `
L54:     __label__4  linux ready for prime time , intel says , despite all the linux hype , the open-source movement has yet to make a huge splash in the desktop market . that may be about to change , thanks to chipmaking giant intel corp .
L55:     __label__2  bowled by the slower one again , kolkata , november 14 the past caught up with sourav ganguly as the indian skippers return to international cricket was short lived .
L56:     `
L57: ###### Note
L58: 
L59: The order of labels within the sentence doesn't matter.
L60: 
L61: Upload the training file under the train channel, and optionally upload the validation file under the validation channel.
L62: ##### Train with Augmented Manifest Text Format
L63: Supervised mode for CPU instances also supports the augmented manifest format, which enables you to do training in pipe mode without needing to create RecordIO files. While using the format, an S3 manifest file needs to be generated that contains the list of sentences and their corresponding labels. The manifest file format should be in cite11†JSON Lines†jsonlines.org format in which each line represents one sample.
L64: The sentences are specified using the `source` tag and the label can be specified using the `label` tag. Both `source` and `label` tags should be provided under the `AttributeNames` parameter value as specified in the request.
L65: 
L66:     `{"source":"linux ready for prime time , intel says , despite all the linux hype", "label":1}
L67:     {"source":"bowled by the slower one again , kolkata , november 14 the past caught up with sourav ganguly", "label":2}`
L68: Multi-label training is also supported by specifying a JSON array of labels.
L69: 
L70:     `{"source":"linux ready for prime time , intel says , despite all the linux hype", "label": [1, 3]}
L71:     {"source":"bowled by the slower one again , kolkata , november 14 the past caught up with sourav ganguly", "label": [2, 4, 5]}`
L72: 
L73: For more information on augmented manifest files, see cite12†Augmented Manifest Files for Training Jobs .
L74: ### Model Artifacts and Inference
L75: #### Model Artifacts for the Word2Vec Algorithm
L76: For Word2Vec training, the model artifacts consist of vectors.txt, which contains words-to-vectors mapping, and vectors.bin, a binary used by BlazingText for hosting, inference, or both. vectors.txt stores the vectors in a format that is compatible with other tools like Gensim and Spacy. For example, a Gensim user can run the following commands to load the vectors.txt file:
L77: 
L78:     `from gensim.models import KeyedVectors
L79:     word_vectors = KeyedVectors.load_word2vec_format('vectors.txt', binary=False)
L80:     word_vectors.most_similar(positive=['woman', 'king'], negative=['man'])
L81:     word_vectors.doesnt_match("breakfast cereal dinner lunch".split())`
L82: If the evaluation parameter is set to `True`, an additional file, eval.json, is created. This file contains the similarity evaluation results (using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients) on WS-353 dataset. The number of words from the WS-353 dataset that aren't there in the training corpus are reported.
L83: For inference requests, the model accepts a JSON file containing a list of strings and returns a list of vectors. If the word is not found in vocabulary, inference returns a vector of zeros. If subwords is set to `True` during training, the model is able to generate vectors for out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words.
L84: ##### Sample JSON Request
L85: 
L86: Mime-type:` application/json`
L87: 
L88:     `{
L89:     "instances": ["word1", "word2", "word3"]
L90:     }`
L91: #### Model Artifacts for the Text Classification Algorithm
L92: 
L93: Training with supervised outputs creates a model.bin file that can be consumed by BlazingText hosting. For inference, the BlazingText model accepts a JSON file containing a list of sentences and returns a list of corresponding predicted labels and probability scores. Each sentence is expected to be a string with space-separated tokens, words, or both.
L94: ##### Sample JSON Request
L95: 
L96: Mime-type:` application/json`
L97: 
L98:     `{
L99:      "instances": ["the movie was excellent", "i did not like the plot ."]
L100:     }`
L101: 
L102: By default, the server returns only one prediction, the one with the highest probability. For retrieving the top k predictions, you can set k in the configuration, as follows:
L103: 
L104:     `{
L105:      "instances": ["the movie was excellent", "i did not like the plot ."],
L106:      "configuration": {"k": 2}
L107:     }`
L108: For BlazingText, the` content-type` and `accept` parameters must be equal. For batch transform, they both need to be `application/jsonlines`. If they differ, the `Accept` field is ignored. The format for input follows:
L109: 
L110:     `content-type: application/jsonlines
L111: 
L112:     {"source": "source_0"}
L113:     {"source": "source_1"}
L114: 
L115:     if you need to pass the value of k for top-k, then you can do it in the following way:
L116: 
L117:     {"source": "source_0", "k": 2}
L118:     {"source": "source_1", "k": 3}`
L119: The format for output follows:
L120: 
L121:     `accept: application/jsonlines
L122: 
L123: 
L124:     {"prob": [prob_1], "label": ["__label__1"]}
L125:     {"prob": [prob_1], "label": ["__label__1"]}

L127:     If you have passed the value of k to be more than 1, then response will be in this format:
L128:

L131: For both supervised (text classification) and unsupervised (Word2Vec) modes, the binaries (*.bin) produced by BlazingText can be cross-consumed by fastText and vice versa. You can use binaries produced by BlazingText by fastText. Likewise, you can host the model binaries created with fastText using BlazingText.
L132: Here is an example of how to use a model generated with BlazingText with fastText:
L133: 
L134:     `
L135:     #Download the model artifact from S3
L136:     aws s3 cp s3://<YOUR_S3_BUCKET>/<PREFIX>/model.tar.gz model.tar.gz
L137: 
L138:     #Unzip the model archive
L139:     tar -xzf model.tar.gz
L140: 
L141:     #Use the model archive with fastText
L142:     fasttext predict ./model.bin test.txt`
L143: 
L144: However, the binaries are only supported when training on CPU and single GPU; training on multi-GPU will not produce binaries.
L145: ## EC2 Instance Recommendation for the BlazingText Algorithm
L146: 
L147: For `cbow` and `skipgram` modes, BlazingText supports single CPU and single GPU instances. Both of these modes support learning of `subwords` embeddings. To achieve the highest speed without compromising accuracy, we recommend that you use an ml.p3.2xlarge instance.
L148: For `batch_skipgram` mode, BlazingText supports single or multiple CPU instances. When training on multiple instances, set the value of the `S3DataDistributionType` field of the cite13†`S3DataSource` object that you pass to cite14†`CreateTrainingJob` to `FullyReplicated`. BlazingText takes care of distributing data across machines.
L149: For the supervised text classification mode, a C5 instance is recommended if the training dataset is less than 2 GB. For larger datasets, use an instance with a single GPU. BlazingText supports P2, P3, G4dn, and G5 instances for training and inference.

For instructions for creating and accessing Jupyter notebook instances that you can use to run the example in SageMaker AI, see cite16†Amazon SageMaker notebook instances .

L75: The classes in the cite67†`sklearn.feature_selection` module can be used for feature selection/dimensionality reduction on sample sets, either to improve estimators’ accuracy scores or to boost their performance on very high-dimensional datasets.
L76: ## 1.13.1. Removing features with low variancecite68†# L77: 
L78: cite69†`VarianceThreshold` is a simple baseline approach to feature selection. It removes all features whose variance doesn’t meet some threshold. By default, it removes all zero-variance features, i.e. features that have the same value in all samples.
L79: As an example, suppose that we have a dataset with boolean features, and we want to remove all features that are either one or zero (on or off) in more than 80% of the samples. Boolean features are Bernoulli random variables, and the variance of such variables is given by
L80: 
L81: \[\mathrm{Var}[X] = p(1 - p)\]
L82: so we can select using the threshold `.8 * (1 - .8)`:
L83: 
L84:     >>> from sklearn.feature_selection import VarianceThreshold
L85:     >>> X = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1]]
L86:     >>> sel = VarianceThreshold(threshold=(.8 * (1 - .8)))
L87:     >>> sel.fit_transform(X)
L88:     array([[0, 1],
L89:            [1, 0],
L90:            [0, 0],
L91:            [1, 1],
L92:            [1, 0],
L93:            [1, 1]])
L94: As expected, `VarianceThreshold` has removed the first column, which has a probability \(p = 5/6 > .8\) of containing a zero.
L95: ## 1.13.2. Univariate feature selectioncite70†# L96: 
L97: Univariate feature selection works by selecting the best features based on univariate statistical tests. It can be seen as a preprocessing step to an estimator. Scikit-learn exposes feature selection routines as objects that implement the `transform` method:
L98: 
L99:   * cite71†`SelectKBest` removes all but the \(k\) highest scoring features
L100: 
L101:   * cite72†`SelectPercentile` removes all but a user-specified highest scoring percentage of features
L102:   * using common univariate statistical tests for each feature: false positive rate cite73†`SelectFpr` , false discovery rate cite74†`SelectFdr` , or family wise error cite75†`SelectFwe` .
L103: 
L104:   * cite76†`GenericUnivariateSelect` allows to perform univariate feature selection with a configurable strategy. This allows to select the best univariate selection strategy with hyper-parameter search estimator.
L105: For instance, we can use an F-test to retrieve the two best features for a dataset as follows:
L106: 
L107:     >>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
L108:     >>> from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest
L109:     >>> from sklearn.feature_selection import f_classif
L110:     >>> X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
L111:     >>> X.shape
L112:     (150, 4)
L113:     >>> X_new = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=2).fit_transform(X, y)
L114:     >>> X_new.shape
L115:     (150, 2)
L116: These objects take as input a scoring function that returns univariate scores and p-values (or only scores for cite71†`SelectKBest` and cite72†`SelectPercentile` ):
L117: 
L118:   * For regression: cite77†`r_regression` , cite78†`f_regression` , cite79†`mutual_info_regression` L119: 
L120:   * For classification: cite80†`chi2` , cite81†`f_classif` , cite82†`mutual_info_classif` L121: The methods based on F-test estimate the degree of linear dependency between two random variables. On the other hand, mutual information methods can capture any kind of statistical dependency, but being nonparametric, they require more samples for accurate estimation. Note that the \(\chi^2\)-test should only be applied to non-negative features, such as frequencies.
L122: 
L123: Feature selection with sparse data
L124: If you use sparse data (i.e. data represented as sparse matrices), cite80†`chi2` , cite79†`mutual_info_regression` , cite82†`mutual_info_classif` will deal with the data without making it dense.
L125: 
L126: Warning
L127: 
L128: Beware not to use a regression scoring function with a classification problem, you will get useless results.
L129: 
L130: Note
L131: The cite72†`SelectPercentile` and cite71†`SelectKBest` support unsupervised feature selection as well. One needs to provide a `score_func` where `y=None`. The `score_func` should use internally `X` to compute the scores.
L132: 
L133: Examples
L134: 
L135:   * cite83†Univariate Feature Selection L136: 
L137:   * cite84†Comparison of F-test and mutual information L138: ## 1.13.3. Recursive feature eliminationcite85†# L139: Given an external estimator that assigns weights to features (e.g., the coefficients of a linear model), the goal of recursive feature elimination (cite86†`RFE` ) is to select features by recursively considering smaller and smaller sets of features. First, the estimator is trained on the initial set of features and the importance of each feature is obtained either through any specific attribute (such as `coef_`, `feature_importances_`) or callable.
L140: Then, the least important features are pruned from the current set of features. That procedure is recursively repeated on the pruned set until the desired number of features to select is eventually reached.
L141: cite87†`RFECV` performs RFE in a cross-validation loop to find the optimal number of features. In more details, the number of features selected is tuned automatically by fitting an cite86†`RFE` selector on the different cross-validation splits (provided by the `cv` parameter). The performance of the cite86†`RFE` selector is evaluated using `scorer` for different numbers of selected features and aggregated together.
L142: Finally, the scores are averaged across folds and the number of features selected is set to the number of features that maximize the cross-validation score.
L143: Examples
L144: 
L145:   * cite88†Recursive feature elimination : A recursive feature elimination example showing the relevance of pixels in a digit classification task.
L146: 
L147:   * cite89†Recursive feature elimination with cross-validation : A recursive feature elimination example with automatic tuning of the number of features selected with cross-validation.
L148: ## 1.13.4. Feature selection using SelectFromModelcite90†# L149: cite91†`SelectFromModel` is a meta-transformer that can be used alongside any estimator that assigns importance to each feature through a specific attribute (such as `coef_`, `feature_importances_`) or via an `importance_getter` callable after fitting. The features are considered unimportant and removed if the corresponding importance of the feature values is below the provided `threshold` parameter.
L150: Apart from specifying the threshold numerically, there are built-in heuristics for finding a threshold using a string argument. Available heuristics are “mean”, “median” and float multiples of these like “0.1*mean”. In combination with the `threshold` criteria, one can use the `max_features` parameter to set a limit on the number of features to select.
L151: For examples on how it is to be used refer to the sections below.
L152: 
L153: Examples
L154: 
L155:   * cite92†Model-based and sequential feature selection L156: ### 1.13.4.1. L1-based feature selectioncite93†# L157: cite94†Linear models penalized with the L1 norm have sparse solutions: many of their estimated coefficients are zero. When the goal is to reduce the dimensionality of the data to use with another classifier, they can be used along with cite91†`SelectFromModel` to select the non-zero coefficients. In particular, sparse estimators useful for this purpose are the cite95†`Lasso` for regression, and of cite96†`LogisticRegression` and cite97†`LinearSVC` for classification:
L158: 
L159:     >>> from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
L160:     >>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
L161:     >>> from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectFromModel
L162:     >>> X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
L163:     >>> X.shape
L164:     (150, 4)
L165:     >>> lsvc = LinearSVC(C=0.01, penalty="l1", dual=False).fit(X, y)
L166:     >>> model = SelectFromModel(lsvc, prefit=True)
L167:     >>> X_new = model.transform(X)
L168:     >>> X_new.shape
L169:     (150, 3)
L170: With SVMs and logistic regression, the parameter C controls the sparsity: the smaller C the fewer features selected. With Lasso, the higher the alpha parameter, the fewer features selected.
L171: 
L172: Examples
L173: 
L174:   * cite98†Lasso on dense and sparse data .
L175: 
L176: L1-recovery and compressive sensingcite99†# L177: For a good choice of alpha, the cite100†Lasso can fully recover the exact set of non-zero variables using only few observations, provided certain specific conditions are met. In particular, the number of samples should be “sufficiently large”, or L1 models will perform at random, where “sufficiently large” depends on the number of non-zero coefficients, the logarithm of the number of features, the amount of noise, the smallest absolute value of non-zero coefficients, and the structure of the design matrix X.
L178: In addition, the design matrix must display certain specific properties, such as not being too correlated. On the use of Lasso for sparse signal recovery, see this example on compressive sensing: cite101†Compressive sensing: tomography reconstruction with L1 prior (Lasso) .
L179: There is no general rule to select an alpha parameter for recovery of non-zero coefficients. It can be set by cross-validation (cite102†`LassoCV` or cite103†`LassoLarsCV` ), though this may lead to under-penalized models: including a small number of non-relevant variables is not detrimental to prediction score. BIC (cite104†`LassoLarsIC` ) tends, on the opposite, to set high values of alpha.
L180: 
L181: References
L182: 
L183: Richard G. Baraniuk cite105†“Compressive Sensing”†doi.org , IEEE Signal Processing Magazine [120] July 2007
L184: ### 1.13.4.2. Tree-based feature selectioncite106†# L185: Tree-based estimators (see the cite107†`sklearn.tree` module and forest of trees in the cite108†`sklearn.ensemble` module) can be used to compute impurity-based feature importances, which in turn can be used to discard irrelevant features (when coupled with the cite91†`SelectFromModel` meta-transformer):
L186: 
L187:     >>> from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesClassifier
L188:     >>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
L189:     >>> from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectFromModel
L190:     >>> X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
L191:     >>> X.shape
L192:     (150, 4)
L193:     >>> clf = ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=50)
L194:     >>> clf = clf.fit(X, y)
L195:     >>> clf.feature_importances_
L196:     array([ 0.04,  0.05,  0.4,  0.4])
L197:     >>> model = SelectFromModel(clf, prefit=True)
L198:     >>> X_new = model.transform(X)
L199:     >>> X_new.shape
L200:     (150, 2)
L201: Examples
L202: 
L203:   * cite109†Feature importances with a forest of trees : example on synthetic data showing the recovery of the actually meaningful features.
L204: 
L205:   * cite110†Permutation Importance vs Random Forest Feature Importance (MDI) : example discussing the caveats of using impurity-based feature importances as a proxy for feature relevance.
L206: ## 1.13.5. Sequential Feature Selectioncite111†# L207: 
L208: Sequential Feature Selection cite112†[sfs] (SFS) is available in the cite113†`SequentialFeatureSelector` transformer. SFS can be either forward or backward:
L209: Forward-SFS is a greedy procedure that iteratively finds the best new feature to add to the set of selected features. Concretely, we initially start with zero features and find the one feature that maximizes a cross-validated score when an estimator is trained on this single feature. Once that first feature is selected, we repeat the procedure by adding a new feature to the set of selected features.
L210: The procedure stops when the desired number of selected features is reached, as determined by the `n_features_to_select` parameter.
L211: Backward-SFS follows the same idea but works in the opposite direction: instead of starting with no features and greedily adding features, we start with all the features and greedily remove features from the set. The `direction` parameter controls whether forward or backward SFS is used.
L212: 
L213: Details on Sequential Feature Selectioncite114†# L214: In general, forward and backward selection do not yield equivalent results. Also, one may be much faster than the other depending on the requested number of selected features: if we have 10 features and ask for 7 selected features, forward selection would need to perform 7 iterations while backward selection would only need to perform 3.
L215: SFS differs from cite86†`RFE` and cite91†`SelectFromModel` in that it does not require the underlying model to expose a `coef_` or `feature_importances_` attribute. It may however be slower considering that more models need to be evaluated, compared to the other approaches.
L216: For example in backward selection, the iteration going from `m` features to `m - 1` features using k-fold cross-validation requires fitting `m * k` models, while cite86†`RFE` would require only a single fit, and cite91†`SelectFromModel` always just does a single fit and requires no iterations.
L217: References
L218: 
L219: [cite115†sfs ]
L220: 
L221: Ferri et al, cite116†Comparative study of techniques for large-scale feature selection†doi.org .
L222: 
L223: Examples
L224: 
L225:   * cite92†Model-based and sequential feature selection L226: ## 1.13.6. Feature selection as part of a pipelinecite117†# L227: 
L228: Feature selection is usually used as a pre-processing step before doing the actual learning. The recommended way to do this in scikit-learn is to use a cite118†`Pipeline` :
L229: 
L230:     clf = Pipeline([
L231:       ('feature_selection', SelectFromModel(LinearSVC(penalty="l1"))),
L232:       ('classification', RandomForestClassifier())
L233:     ])
L234:     clf.fit(X, y)
L235: In this snippet we make use of a cite97†`LinearSVC` coupled with cite91†`SelectFromModel` to evaluate feature importances and select the most relevant features. Then, a cite119†`RandomForestClassifier` is trained on the transformed output, i.e. using only relevant features. You can perform similar operations with the other feature selection methods and also classifiers that provide a way to evaluate feature importances of course. See the cite118†`Pipeline` examples for more details.

L4: cite1†Maintenance cite2†Machine Learning with the SageMaker Python SDK L5: # Amazon SageMaker notebook instances
L6: An Amazon SageMaker notebook instance is a machine learning (ML) compute instance running the Jupyter Notebook application. One of the best ways for machine learning (ML) practitioners to use Amazon SageMaker AI is to train and deploy ML models using SageMaker notebook instances.
L7: The SageMaker notebook instances help create the environment by initiating Jupyter servers on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and providing preconfigured kernels with the following packages: the Amazon SageMaker Python SDK, AWS SDK for Python (Boto3), AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), Conda, Pandas, deep learning framework libraries, and other libraries for data science and machine learning.
L8: Use Jupyter notebooks in your notebook instance to:
L9: 
L10:   * prepare and process data
L11: 
L12:   * write code to train models
L13: 
L14:   * deploy models to SageMaker hosting
L15: 
L16:   * test or validate your models
L17: 
L18: For information about pricing with Amazon SageMaker notebook instance, see cite3†Amazon SageMaker Pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L19: ## Maintenance
L20: 
L21: SageMaker AI updates the underlying software for Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instances at least once every 90 days. Some maintenance updates, such as operating system upgrades, may require your application to be taken offline for a short period of time. It is not possible to perform any operations during this period while the underlying software is being updated. We recommend that you restart your notebooks at least once every 30 days to automatically consume patches.
L22: If the notebook instance isn't updated and is running unsecure software, SageMaker AI might periodically update the instance as part of regular maintenance. During these updates, data outside of the folder `/home/ec2-user/SageMaker` is not persisted.
L23: 
L24: For more information, contact cite4†AWS Support†aws.amazon.com .
L25: ## Machine Learning with the SageMaker Python SDK
L26: To train, validate, deploy, and evaluate an ML model in a SageMaker notebook instance, use the SageMaker Python SDK. The SageMaker Python SDK abstracts AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) and SageMaker API operations.
L27: It enables you to integrate with and orchestrate other AWS services, such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for saving data and model artifacts, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) for importing and servicing the ML models, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) for training and inference.
L28: You can also take advantage of SageMaker AI features that help you deal with every stage of a complete ML cycle: data labeling, data preprocessing, model training, model deployment, evaluation on prediction performance, and monitoring the quality of model in production.
L29: 
L30: If you're a first-time SageMaker AI user, we recommend you to use the SageMaker Python SDK, following the end-to-end ML tutorial. To find the open source documentation, see the cite5†Amazon SageMaker Python SDK†sagemaker.readthedocs.io .

External Resources, Videos and Talks L73: # 8.4. Imputation of missing valuescite66†# L74: For various reasons, many real world datasets contain missing values, often encoded as blanks, NaNs or other placeholders. Such datasets however are incompatible with scikit-learn estimators which assume that all values in an array are numerical, and that all have and hold meaning. A basic strategy to use incomplete datasets is to discard entire rows and/or columns containing missing values. However, this comes at the price of losing data which may be valuable (even though incomplete).
L75: A better strategy is to impute the missing values, i.e., to infer them from the known part of the data. See the glossary entry on cite67†imputation .
L76: ## 8.4.1. Univariate vs. Multivariate Imputationcite68†# L77: 
L78: One type of imputation algorithm is univariate, which imputes values in the i-th feature dimension using only non-missing values in that feature dimension (e.g. cite69†`SimpleImputer` ). By contrast, multivariate imputation algorithms use the entire set of available feature dimensions to estimate the missing values (e.g. cite70†`IterativeImputer` ).
L79: ## 8.4.2. Univariate feature imputationcite71†# L80: 
L81: The cite69†`SimpleImputer` class provides basic strategies for imputing missing values. Missing values can be imputed with a provided constant value, or using the statistics (mean, median or most frequent) of each column in which the missing values are located. This class also allows for different missing values encodings.
L82: The following snippet demonstrates how to replace missing values, encoded as `np.nan`, using the mean value of the columns (axis 0) that contain the missing values:
L83: 
L84:     >>> import numpy as np
L85:     >>> from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
L86:     >>> imp = SimpleImputer(missing_values=np.nan, strategy='mean')
L87:     >>> imp.fit([[1, 2], [np.nan, 3], [7, 6]])
L88:     SimpleImputer()
L89:     >>> X = [[np.nan, 2], [6, np.nan], [7, 6]]
L90:     >>> print(imp.transform(X))
L91:     [[4.          2.        ]
L92:      [6.          3.666]
L93:      [7.          6.        ]]
L94: The cite69†`SimpleImputer` class also supports sparse matrices:
L95: 
L96:     >>> import scipy.sparse as sp
L97:     >>> X = sp.csc_array([[1, 2], [0, -1], [8, 4]])
L98:     >>> imp = SimpleImputer(missing_values=-1, strategy='mean')
L99:     >>> imp.fit(X)
L100:     SimpleImputer(missing_values=-1)
L101:     >>> X_test = sp.csc_array([[-1, 2], [6, -1], [7, 6]])
L102:     >>> print(imp.transform(X_test).toarray())
L103:     [[3. 2.]
L104:      [6. 3.]
L105:      [7. 6.]]
L106: Note that this format is not meant to be used to implicitly store missing values in the matrix because it would densify it at transform time. Missing values encoded by 0 must be used with dense input.
L107: The cite69†`SimpleImputer` class also supports categorical data represented as string values or pandas categoricals when using the `'most_frequent'` or `'constant'` strategy:
L108: 
L109:     >>> import pandas as pd
L110:     >>> df = pd.DataFrame([["a", "x"],
L111:     ...                    [np.nan, "y"],
L112:     ...                    ["a", np.nan],
L113:     ...                    ["b", "y"]], dtype="category")
L114:     ...
L115:     >>> imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")
L116:     >>> print(imp.fit_transform(df))
L117:     [['a' 'x']
L118:      ['a' 'y']
L119:      ['a' 'y']
L120:      ['b' 'y']]
L121: For another example on usage, see cite72†Imputing missing values before building an estimator .
L122: ## 8.4.3. Multivariate feature imputationcite73†# L123: A more sophisticated approach is to use the cite70†`IterativeImputer` class, which models each feature with missing values as a function of other features, and uses that estimate for imputation. It does so in an iterated round-robin fashion: at each step, a feature column is designated as output `y` and the other feature columns are treated as inputs `X`. A regressor is fit on `(X, y)` for known `y`. Then, the regressor is used to predict the missing values of `y`.
L124: This is done for each feature in an iterative fashion, and then is repeated for `max_iter` imputation rounds. The results of the final imputation round are returned.
L125: Note
L126: This estimator is still experimental for now: default parameters or details of behaviour might change without any deprecation cycle. Resolving the following issues would help stabilize cite70†`IterativeImputer` : convergence criteria (cite74†#14338†github.com ) and default estimators (cite75†#13286†github.com ). To use it, you need to explicitly import `enable_iterative_imputer`.
L127: 
L128:     >>> import numpy as np
L129:     >>> from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer
L130:     >>> from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer
L131:     >>> imp = IterativeImputer(max_iter=10, random_state=0)
L132:     >>> imp.fit([[1, 2], [3, 6], [4, 8], [np.nan, 3], [7, np.nan]])
L133:     IterativeImputer(random_state=0)
L134:     >>> X_test = [[np.nan, 2], [6, np.nan], [np.nan, 6]]
L135:     >>> # the model learns that the second feature is double the first
L136:     >>> print(np.round(imp.transform(X_test)))
L137:     [[ 1.  2.]
L138:      [ 6. 12.]
L139:      [ 3.  6.]]
L140: Both cite69†`SimpleImputer` and cite70†`IterativeImputer` can be used in a Pipeline as a way to build a composite estimator that supports imputation. See cite72†Imputing missing values before building an estimator .
L141: ### 8.4.3.1. Flexibility of IterativeImputercite76†# L142: There are many well-established imputation packages in the R data science ecosystem: Amelia, mi, mice, missForest, etc. missForest is popular, and turns out to be a particular instance of different sequential imputation algorithms that can all be implemented with cite70†`IterativeImputer` by passing in different regressors to be used for predicting missing feature values. In the case of missForest, this regressor is a Random Forest. See cite77†Imputing missing values with variants of IterativeImputer .
L143: ### 8.4.3.2. Multiple vs. Single Imputationcite78†# L144: In the statistics community, it is common practice to perform multiple imputations, generating, for example, `m` separate imputations for a single feature matrix. Each of these `m` imputations is then put through the subsequent analysis pipeline (e.g. feature engineering, clustering, regression, classification). The `m` final analysis results (e.g.
L145: held-out validation errors) allow the data scientist to obtain understanding of how analytic results may differ as a consequence of the inherent uncertainty caused by the missing values. The above practice is called multiple imputation.
L146: Our implementation of cite70†`IterativeImputer` was inspired by the R MICE package (Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations) cite79†[1] , but differs from it by returning a single imputation instead of multiple imputations. However, cite70†`IterativeImputer` can also be used for multiple imputations by applying it repeatedly to the same dataset with different random seeds when `sample_posterior=True`. See cite80†[2] , chapter 4 for more discussion on multiple vs. single imputations.
L147: It is still an open problem as to how useful single vs. multiple imputation is in the context of prediction and classification when the user is not interested in measuring uncertainty due to missing values.
L148: 
L149: Note that a call to the `transform` method of cite70†`IterativeImputer` is not allowed to change the number of samples. Therefore multiple imputations cannot be achieved by a single call to `transform`.
L150: 
L151: References
L152: 
L153: [cite81†1 ]
L154: cite82†Stef van Buuren, Karin Groothuis-Oudshoorn (2011). “mice: Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations in R”. Journal of Statistical Software 45: 1-67.†www.jstatsoft.org L155: 
L156: [cite83†2 ]
L157: 
L158: Roderick J A Little and Donald B Rubin (1986). “Statistical Analysis with Missing Data”. John Wiley & Sons, Inc., New York, NY, USA.
L159: ## 8.4.4. Nearest neighbors imputationcite84†# L160: The cite85†`KNNImputer` class provides imputation for filling in missing values using the k-Nearest Neighbors approach. By default, a euclidean distance metric that supports missing values, cite86†`nan_euclidean_distances` , is used to find the nearest neighbors. Each missing feature is imputed using values from `n_neighbors` nearest neighbors that have a value for the feature. The feature of the neighbors are averaged uniformly or weighted by distance to each neighbor.
L161: If a sample has more than one feature missing, then the neighbors for that sample can be different depending on the particular feature being imputed. When the number of available neighbors is less than `n_neighbors` and there are no defined distances to the training set, the training set average for that feature is used during imputation. If there is at least one neighbor with a defined distance, the weighted or unweighted average of the remaining neighbors will be used during imputation.
L162: If a feature is always missing in training, it is removed during `transform`. For more information on the methodology, see ref. cite87†[OL2001] .
L163: The following snippet demonstrates how to replace missing values, encoded as `np.nan`, using the mean feature value of the two nearest neighbors of samples with missing values:
L164: 
L165:     >>> import numpy as np
L166:     >>> from sklearn.impute import KNNImputer
L167:     >>> nan = np.nan
L168:     >>> X = [[1, 2, nan], [3, 4, 3], [nan, 6, 5], [8, 8, 7]]
L169:     >>> imputer = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=2, weights="uniform")
L170:     >>> imputer.fit_transform(X)
L171:     array([[1. , 2. , 4. ],
L172:            [3. , 4. , 3. ],
L173:            [5.5, 6. , 5. ],
L174:            [8. , 8. , 7. ]])
L175: For another example on usage, see cite72†Imputing missing values before building an estimator .
L176: 
L177: References
L178: 
L179: [cite88†OL2001 ]
L180: 
L181: cite89†Olga Troyanskaya, Michael Cantor, Gavin Sherlock, Pat Brown, Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, David Botstein and Russ B. Altman, Missing value estimation methods for DNA microarrays, BIOINFORMATICS Vol. 17 no. 6, 2001 Pages 520-525.†academic.oup.com L182: ## 8.4.5. Keeping the number of features constantcite90†# L183: 
L184: By default, the scikit-learn imputers will drop fully empty features, i.e. columns containing only missing values. For instance:
L185: 
L186:     >>> imputer = SimpleImputer()
L187:     >>> X = np.array([[np.nan, 1], [np.nan, 2], [np.nan, 3]])
L188:     >>> imputer.fit_transform(X)
L189:     array([[1.],
L190:            [2.],
L191:            [3.]])
L192: The first feature in `X` containing only `np.nan` was dropped after the imputation. While this feature will not help in predictive setting, dropping the columns will change the shape of `X` which could be problematic when using imputers in a more complex machine-learning pipeline. The parameter `keep_empty_features` offers the option to keep the empty features by imputing with a constant value. In most of the cases, this constant value is zero:
L193: 
L194:     >>> imputer.set_params(keep_empty_features=True)
L195:     SimpleImputer(keep_empty_features=True)
L196:     >>> imputer.fit_transform(X)
L197:     array([[0., 1.],
L198:            [0., 2.],
L199:            [0., 3.]])
L200: ## 8.4.6. Marking imputed valuescite91†# L201: The cite92†`MissingIndicator` transformer is useful to transform a dataset into corresponding binary matrix indicating the presence of missing values in the dataset. This transformation is useful in conjunction with imputation. When using imputation, preserving the information about which values had been missing can be informative.
L202: Note that both the cite69†`SimpleImputer` and cite70†`IterativeImputer` have the boolean parameter `add_indicator` (`False` by default) which when set to `True` provides a convenient way of stacking the output of the cite92†`MissingIndicator` transformer with the output of the imputer.
L203: `NaN` is usually used as the placeholder for missing values. However, it enforces the data type to be float. The parameter `missing_values` allows to specify other placeholder such as integer. In the following example, we will use `-1` as missing values:
L204: 
L205:     >>> from sklearn.impute import MissingIndicator
L206:     >>> X = np.array([[-1, -1, 1, 3],
L207:     ...               [4, -1, 0, -1],
L208:     ...               [8, -1, 1, 0]])
L209:     >>> indicator = MissingIndicator(missing_values=-1)
L210:     >>> mask_missing_values_only = indicator.fit_transform(X)
L211:     >>> mask_missing_values_only
L212:     array([[ True,  True, False],
L213:            [False,  True,  True],
L214:            [False,  True, False]])
L215: The `features` parameter is used to choose the features for which the mask is constructed. By default, it is `'missing-only'` which returns the imputer mask of the features containing missing values at `fit` time:
L216: 
L217:     >>> indicator.features_
L218:     array([0, 1, 3])
L219: The `features` parameter can be set to `'all'` to return all features whether or not they contain missing values:
L220: 
L221:     >>> indicator = MissingIndicator(missing_values=-1, features="all")
L222:     >>> mask_all = indicator.fit_transform(X)
L223:     >>> mask_all
L224:     array([[ True,  True, False, False],
L225:            [False,  True, False,  True],
L226:            [False,  True, False, False]])
L227:     >>> indicator.features_
L228:     array([0, 1, 2, 3])
L229: When using the cite92†`MissingIndicator` in a cite93†`Pipeline` , be sure to use the cite94†`FeatureUnion` or cite95†`ColumnTransformer` to add the indicator features to the regular features. First we obtain the `iris` dataset, and add some missing values to it.
L230: 
L231:     >>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
L232:     >>> from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer, MissingIndicator
L233:     >>> from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
L234:     >>> from sklearn.pipeline import FeatureUnion, make_pipeline
L235:     >>> from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
L236:     >>> X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
L237:     >>> mask = np.random.randint(0, 2, size=X.shape).astype(bool)
L238:     >>> X[mask] = np.nan
L239:     >>> X_train, X_test, y_train, _ = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=100,
L240:     ...                                                random_state=0)
L241: Now we create a cite94†`FeatureUnion` . All features will be imputed using cite69†`SimpleImputer` , in order to enable classifiers to work with this data. Additionally, it adds the indicator variables from cite92†`MissingIndicator` .
L242: 
L243:     >>> transformer = FeatureUnion(
L244:     ...     transformer_list=[
L245:     ...         ('features', SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')),
L246:     ...         ('indicators', MissingIndicator())])
L247:     >>> transformer = transformer.fit(X_train, y_train)
L248:     >>> results = transformer.transform(X_test)
L249:     >>> results.shape
L250:     (100, 8)
L251: Of course, we cannot use the transformer to make any predictions. We should wrap this in a cite93†`Pipeline` with a classifier (e.g., a cite96†`DecisionTreeClassifier` ) to be able to make predictions.
L252: 
L253:     >>> clf = make_pipeline(transformer, DecisionTreeClassifier())
L254:     >>> clf = clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
L255:     >>> results = clf.predict(X_test)
L256:     >>> results.shape
L257:     (100,)
L258: ## 8.4.7. Estimators that handle NaN valuescite97†# L259:

L11: # What Is Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL Applications?
L12: 
L13: With Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL Applications, you can process and analyze streaming data using standard SQL. The service enables you to quickly author and run powerful SQL code against streaming sources to perform time series analytics, feed real-time dashboards, and create real-time metrics.
L14: To get started with Kinesis Data Analytics, you create a Kinesis Data Analytics application that continuously reads and processes streaming data. The service supports ingesting data from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose streaming sources. Then, you author your SQL code using the interactive editor and test it with live streaming data. You can also configure destinations where you want Kinesis Data Analytics to send the results.
L15: Kinesis Data Analytics supports Amazon Data Firehose (Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon OpenSearch Service, and Splunk), AWS Lambda, and Amazon Kinesis Data Streams as destinations.
L16: ## When Should I Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics?
L17: 
L18: Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics enables you to quickly author SQL code that continuously reads, processes, and stores data in near real time. Using standard SQL queries on the streaming data, you can construct applications that transform and provide insights into your data. Following are some of example scenarios for using Kinesis Data Analytics:
L19:   * Generate time-series analytics – You can calculate metrics over time windows, and then stream values to Amazon S3 or Amazon Redshift through a Kinesis data delivery stream.
L20: 
L21:   * Feed real-time dashboards – You can send aggregated and processed streaming data results downstream to feed real-time dashboards.
L22: 
L23:   * Create real-time metrics – You can create custom metrics and triggers for use in real-time monitoring, notifications, and alarms.
L24: For information about the SQL language elements that are supported by Kinesis Data Analytics, see cite4†Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics SQL Reference .
L25: ## Are You a First-Time User of Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics?
L26: 
L27: If you are a first-time user of Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics, we recommend that you read the following sections in order:
L28: 
L29:   1. Read the How It Works section of this guide. This section introduces various Kinesis Data Analytics components that you work with to create an end-to-end experience. For more information, see cite5†Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL Applications: How It Works .
L30:   2. Try the Getting Started exercises. For more information, see cite6†Getting Started with Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL Applications .
L31: 
L32:   3. Explore the streaming SQL concepts. For more information, see cite7†Streaming SQL Concepts .
L33: 
L34:   4. Try additional examples. For more information, see cite8†Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL examples .
