L6: 
L7: You can use Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler to import data from the following data sources: Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, and Snowflake. The dataset that you import can include up to 1000 columns.
L8: ###### Topics
L9: 
L10:   * cite1†Import data from Amazon S3 L11: 
L12:   * cite2†Import data from Athena L13: 
L14:   * cite3†Import data from Amazon Redshift L15: 
L16:   * cite4†Import data from Amazon EMR L17: 
L18:   * cite5†Import data from Databricks (JDBC) L19: 
L20:   * cite6†Import data from Salesforce Data Cloud L21: 
L22:   * cite7†Import data from Snowflake L23: 
L24:   * cite8†Import Data From Software as a Service (SaaS) Platforms L25: 
L26:   * cite9†Imported Data Storage L27: 
L28: Some data sources allow you to add multiple data connections:
L29:   * You can connect to multiple Amazon Redshift clusters. Each cluster becomes a data source.
L30: 
L31:   * You can query any Athena database in your account to import data from that database.
L32: 
L33: When you import a dataset from a data source, it appears in your data flow. Data Wrangler automatically infers the data type of each column in your dataset. To modify these types, select the Data types step and select Edit data types.
L34: When you import data from Athena or Amazon Redshift, the imported data is automatically stored in the default SageMaker AI S3 bucket for the AWS Region in which you are using Studio Classic. Additionally, Athena stores data you preview in Data Wrangler in this bucket. To learn more, see cite9†Imported Data Storage .
L35: ###### Important
L36: 
L37: The default Amazon S3 bucket may not have the least permissive security settings, such as bucket policy and server-side encryption (SSE). We strongly recommend that you cite10†Add a Bucket Policy To Restrict Access to Datasets Imported to Data Wrangler .
L38: ###### Important
L39: 
L40: In addition, if you use the managed policy for SageMaker AI, we strongly recommend that you scope it down to the most restrictive policy that allows you to perform your use case. For more information, see cite11†Grant an IAM Role Permission to Use Data Wrangler .
L41: 
L42: All data sources except for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) require you to specify a SQL query to import your data. For each query, you must specify the following:
L43: 
L44:   * Data catalog
L45: 
L46:   * Database
L47: 
L48:   * Table
L49: You can specify the name of the database or the data catalog in either the drop down menus or within the query. The following are example queries:
L50: 
L51:   * `select * from `example-data-catalog-name`.`example-database-name`.`example-table-name`` – The query doesn't use anything specified in the dropdown menus of the user-interface (UI) to run. It queries `example-table-name` within `example-database-name` within `example-data-catalog-name`.
L52:   * `select * from `example-database-name`.`example-table-name`` – The query uses the data catalog that you've specified in the Data catalog dropdown menu to run. It queries `example-table-name` within `example-database-name` within the data catalog that you've specified.
L53:   * `select * from `example-table-name`` – The query requires you to select fields for both the Data catalog and Database name dropdown menus. It queries `example-table-name` within the data catalog within the database and data catalog that you've specified.
L54: 
L55: The link between Data Wrangler and the data source is a connection. You use the connection to import data from your data source.
L56: 
L57: There are the following types of connections:
L58: 
L59:   * Direct
L60: 
L61:   * Cataloged
L62: Data Wrangler always has access to the most recent data in a direct connection. If the data in the data source has been updated, you can use the connection to import the data. For example, if someone adds a file to one of your Amazon S3 buckets, you can import the file.
L63: A cataloged connection is the result of a data transfer. The data in the cataloged connection doesn't necessarily have the most recent data. For example, you might set up a data transfer between Salesforce and Amazon S3. If there's an update to the Salesforce data, you must transfer the data again. You can automate the process of transferring data. For more information about data transfers, see cite8†Import Data From Software as a Service (SaaS) Platforms .
L64: ## Import data from Amazon S3
L65: You can use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) to store and retrieve any amount of data, at any time, from anywhere on the web. You can accomplish these tasks using the AWS Management Console, which is a simple and intuitive web interface, and the Amazon S3 API. If you've stored your dataset locally, we recommend that you add it to an S3 bucket for import into Data Wrangler. To learn how, see cite12†Uploading an object to a bucket in the Amazon Simple Storage Service User Guide.
L66: Data Wrangler uses cite13†S3 Select†aws.amazon.com to allow you to preview your Amazon S3 files in Data Wrangler. You incur standard charges for each file preview. To learn more about pricing, see the Requests & data retrievals tab on cite14†Amazon S3 pricing†aws.amazon.com .
L67: ###### Important
L68: 
L69: If you plan to export a data flow and launch a Data Wrangler job, ingest data into a SageMaker AI feature store, or create a SageMaker AI pipeline, be aware that these integrations require Amazon S3 input data to be located in the same AWS region.
L70: ###### Important
L71: 
L72: If you're importing a CSV file, make sure it meets the following requirements:
L73: 
L74:   * A record in your dataset can't be longer than one line.
L75: 
L76:   * A backslash, `\`, is the only valid escape character.
L77: 
L78:   * Your dataset must use one of the following delimiters:
L79: 
L80:     * Comma – `,`
L81: 
L82:     * Colon – `:`
L83: 
L84:     * Semicolon – `;`
L85: 
L86:     * Pipe – `|`
L87: 
L88:     * Tab – `[TAB]`
L89: 
L90: To save space, you can import compressed CSV files.
L91: Data Wrangler gives you the ability to either import the entire dataset or sample a portion of it. For Amazon S3, it provides the following sampling options:
L92: 
L93:   * None – Import the entire dataset.
L94: 
L95:   * First K – Sample the first K rows of the dataset, where K is an integer that you specify.
L96: 
L97:   * Randomized – Takes a random sample of a size that you specify.
L98: 
L99:   * Stratified – Takes a stratified random sample. A stratified sample preserves the ratio of values in a column.
L100: After you've imported your data, you can also use the sampling transformer to take one or more samples from your entire dataset. For more information about the sampling transformer, see cite15†Sampling .
L101: 
L102: You can use one of the following resource identifiers to import your data:
L103: 
L104:   * An Amazon S3 URI that uses an Amazon S3 bucket or Amazon S3 access point
L105: 
L106:   * An Amazon S3 access point alias
L107: 
L108:   * An Amazon Resource Name (ARN) that uses an Amazon S3 access point or Amazon S3 bucket
L109: Amazon S3 access points are named network endpoints that are attached to the buckets. Each access point has distinct permissions and network controls that you can configure. For more information about access points, see cite16†Managing data access with Amazon S3 access points .
L110: ###### Important
L111: 
L112: If you're using an Amazon Resource Name (ARN) to import your data, it must be for a resource located in the same AWS Region that you're using to access Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic.
L113: You can import either a single file or multiple files as a dataset. You can use the multifile import operation when you have a dataset that is partitioned into separate files. It takes all of the files from an Amazon S3 directory and imports them as a single dataset. For information on the types of files that you can import and how to import them, see the following sections.
L114: 
L115: Single File Import
L116: 
L117: 
L118: You can import single files in the following formats:
L119: 
L120:   * Comma Separated Values (CSV)
L121: 
L122:   * Parquet
L123:   * Javascript Object Notation (JSON)
L124: 
L125:   * Optimized Row Columnar (ORC)
L126: 
L127:   * Image – Data Wrangler uses OpenCV to import images. For more information about supported image formats, see cite17†Image file reading and writing†docs.opencv.org .
L128: For files formatted in JSON, Data Wrangler supports both JSON lines (.jsonl) and JSON documents (.json). When you preview your data, it automatically shows the JSON in tabular format. For nested JSON documents that are larger than 5 MB, Data Wrangler shows the schema for the structure and the arrays as values in the dataset. Use the Flatten structured and Explode array operators to display the nested values in tabular format. For more information, see cite18†Unnest JSON Data and cite19†Explode Array .
L129: When you choose a dataset, you can rename it, specify the file type, and identify the first row as a header.
L130: 
L131: You can import a dataset that you've partitioned into multiple files in an Amazon S3 bucket in a single import step.
L132: ###### To import a dataset into Data Wrangler from a single file that you've stored in Amazon S3:
L133: 
L134:   1. If you are not currently on the Import tab, choose Import.
L135: 
L136:   2. Under Available, choose Amazon S3.
L137: 
L138:   3. From the Import tabular, image, or time-series data from S3, do one of the following:
L139: 
L140:      * Choose an Amazon S3 bucket from the tabular view and navigate to the file that you're importing.
L141:      * For S3 source, specify an Amazon S3 bucket or an Amazon S3 URI and select Go. The Amazon S3 URIs can be in one of the following formats:
L142: 
L143:        * `s3://`amzn-s3-demo-bucket`/`example-prefix`/`example-file``
L144: 
L145:        * `example-access-point`-`aqfqprnstn7aefdfbarligizwgyfouse1a`-s3alias/datasets/`example-file`
L146: 
L147:        * `s3://arn:aws:s3:`AWS-Region`:`111122223333`:accesspoint/`example-prefix`/`example-file``
L148: 
L149:   4. Choose the dataset to open the Import settings pane.
L150:   5. If your CSV file has a header, select the checkbox next to Add header to table.
L151: 
L152:   6. Use the Preview table to preview your dataset. This table shows up to 100 rows.
L153: 
L154:   7. In the Details pane, verify or change the Name and File Type for your dataset. If you add a Name that contains spaces, these spaces are replaced with underscores when your dataset is imported.
L155: 
L156:   8. Specify the sampling configuration that you'd like to use.
L157: 
L158:   9. Choose Import.
L159: 
L160: Multifile Import
L161: The following are the requirements for importing multiple files:
L162: 
L163:   * The files must be in the same folder of your Amazon S3 bucket.
L164: 
L165:   * The files must either share the same header or have no header.
L166: 
L167: Each file must be in one of the following formats:
L168: 
L169:   * CSV
L170: 
L171:   * Parquet
L172: 
L173:   * Optimized Row Columnar (ORC)
L174: 
L175:   * Image – Data Wrangler uses OpenCV to import images. For more information about supported image formats, see cite17†Image file reading and writing†docs.opencv.org .
L176: Use the following procedure to import multiple files.
L177: ###### To import a dataset into Data Wrangler from multiple files that you've stored in an Amazon S3 directory
L178: 
L179:   1. If you are not currently on the Import tab, choose Import.
L180: 
L181:   2. Under Available, choose Amazon S3.
L182: 
L183:   3. From the Import tabular, image, or time-series data from S3, do one of the following:
L184: 
L185:      * Choose an Amazon S3 bucket from the tabular view and navigate to the folder containing the files that you're importing.
L186:      * For S3 source, specify the Amazon S3 bucket or an Amazon S3 URI with your files and select Go. The following are valid URIs:
L187: 
L188:        * `s3://`amzn-s3-demo-bucket`/`example-prefix`/`example-prefix``
L189: 
L190:        * ``example-access-point`-`aqfqprnstn7aefdfbarligizwgyfouse1a`-s3alias/`example-prefix`/`
L191: 
L192:        * `s3://arn:aws:s3:AWS-Region:`111122223333`:accesspoint/`example-prefix``
L193:   4. Select the folder containing the files that you want to import. Each file must be in one of the supported formats. Your files must be the same data type.
L194: 
L195:   5. If your folder contains CSV files with headers, select the checkbox next to First row is header.
L196: 
L197:   6. If your files are nested within other folders, select the checkbox next to Include nested directories.
L198: 
L199:   7. (Optional) Choose Add filename column add a column to the dataset that shows the filename for each observation.
L200:   8. (Optional) By default, Data Wrangler doesn't show you a preview of a folder. You can activate previewing by choosing the blue Preview off button. A preview shows the first 10 rows of the first 10 files in the folder.
L201: 
L202:   9. In the Details pane, verify or change the Name and File Type for your dataset. If you add a Name that contains spaces, these spaces are replaced with underscores when your dataset is imported.
L203: 
L204:   10. Specify the sampling configuration that you'd like to use.
L205:   11. Choose Import dataset.
L206: 
L207: You can also use parameters to import a subset of files that match a pattern. Parameters help you more selectively pick the files that you're importing. To start using parameters, edit the data source and apply them to the path that you're using to import the data. For more information, see cite20†Reusing Data Flows for Different Datasets .
L208: ## Import data from Athena
L209: 
L210: Use Amazon Athena to import your data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) into Data Wrangler. In Athena, you write standard SQL queries to select the data that you're importing from Amazon S3. For more information, see cite21†What is Amazon Athena? L211: You can use the AWS Management Console to set up Amazon Athena. You must create at least one database in Athena before you start running queries. For more information about getting started with Athena, see cite22†Getting started .
L212: 
L213: Athena is directly integrated with Data Wrangler. You can write Athena queries without having to leave the Data Wrangler UI.
L214: 
L215: In addition to writing simple Athena queries in Data Wrangler, you can also use:
L216:   * Athena workgroups for query result management. For more information about workgroups, see cite23†Managing query results .
L217: 
L218:   * Lifecycle configurations for setting data retention periods. For more information about data retention, see cite24†Setting data retention periods .
L219: ### Query Athena within Data Wrangler
L220: ###### Note
L221: 
L222: Data Wrangler does not support federated queries.
L223: 
L224: If you use AWS Lake Formation with Athena, make sure your Lake Formation IAM permissions do not override IAM permissions for the database `sagemaker_data_wrangler`.
L225: 
L226: Data Wrangler gives you the ability to either import the entire dataset or sample a portion of it. For Athena, it provides the following sampling options:
L227: 
L228:   * None – Import the entire dataset.
L229:   * First K – Sample the first K rows of the dataset, where K is an integer that you specify.
L230: 
L231:   * Randomized – Takes a random sample of a size that you specify.
L232: 
L233:   * Stratified – Takes a stratified random sample. A stratified sample preserves the ratio of values in a column.
L234: 
L235: The following procedure shows how to import a dataset from Athena into Data Wrangler.
L236: ###### To import a dataset into Data Wrangler from Athena
L237: 
L238:   1. Sign into cite25†Amazon SageMaker AI Console†console.aws.amazon.com .
L239: 
L240:   2. Choose Studio.
L241: 
L242:   3. Choose Launch app.
L243: 
L244:   4. From the dropdown list, select Studio.
L245: 
L246:   5. Choose the Home icon.
L247: 
L248:   6. Choose Data.
L249: 
L250:   7. Choose Data Wrangler.
L251: 
L252:   8. Choose Import data.
L253: 
L254:   9. Under Available, choose Amazon Athena.
L255: 
L256:   10. For Data Catalog, choose a data catalog.
L257:   11. Use the Database dropdown list to select the database that you want to query. When you select a database, you can preview all tables in your database using the Tables listed under Details.
L258: 
L259:   12. (Optional) Choose Advanced configuration.
L260: 
L261:     1. Choose a Workgroup.
L262: 
L263:     2. If your workgroup hasn't enforced the Amazon S3 output location or if you don't use a workgroup, specify a value for Amazon S3 location of query results.
L264:     3. (Optional) For Data retention period, select the checkbox to set a data retention period and specify the number of days to store the data before it's deleted.
L265: 
L266:     4. (Optional) By default, Data Wrangler saves the connection. You can choose to deselect the checkbox and not save the connection.
L267: 
L268:   13. For Sampling, choose a sampling method. Choose None to turn off sampling.
L269:   14. Enter your query in the query editor and use the Run button to run the query. After a successful query, you can preview your result under the editor.
L270: ###### Note
L271: 
L272: Salesforce data uses the `timestamptz` type. If you're querying the timestamp column that you've imported to Athena from Salesforce, cast the data in the column to the `timestamp` type. The following query casts the timestamp column to the correct type.
L273: 
L274:     `
L275:     # cast column timestamptz_col as timestamp type, and name it as timestamp_col
L276:     select cast(timestamptz_col as timestamp) as timestamp_col from table
L277:                             `
L278:   15. To import the results of your query, select Import.
L279: 
L280: After you complete the preceding procedure, the dataset that you've queried and imported appears in the Data Wrangler flow.
L281: By default, Data Wrangler saves the connection settings as a new connection. When you import your data, the query that you've already specified appears as a new connection. The saved connections store information about the Athena workgroups and Amazon S3 buckets that you're using. When you're connecting to the data source again, you can choose the saved connection.
L282: ### Managing query results
L283: 
L284: Data Wrangler supports using Athena workgroups to manage the query results within an AWS account. You can specify an Amazon S3 output location for each workgroup. You can also specify whether the output of the query can go to different Amazon S3 locations. For more information, see cite26†Using Workgroups to Control Query Access and Costs .
L285: Your workgroup might be configured to enforce the Amazon S3 query output location. You can't change the output location of the query results for those workgroups.
L286: If you don't use a workgroup or specify an output location for your queries, Data Wrangler uses the default Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region in which your Studio Classic instance is located to store Athena query results. It creates temporary tables in this database to move the query output to this Amazon S3 bucket. It deletes these tables after data has been imported; however the database, `sagemaker_data_wrangler`, persists. To learn more, see cite9†Imported Data Storage .
L287: To use Athena workgroups, set up the IAM policy that gives access to workgroups. If you're using a `SageMaker AI-Execution-Role`, we recommend adding the policy to the role. For more information about IAM policies for workgroups, see cite27†IAM policies for accessing workgroups . For example workgroup policies, see cite28†Workgroup example policies .
L288: ### Setting data retention periods
L289: Data Wrangler automatically sets a data retention period for the query results. The results are deleted after the length of the retention period. For example, the default retention period is five days. The results of the query are deleted after five days. This configuration is designed to help you clean up data that you're no longer using. Cleaning up your data prevents unauthorized users from gaining access. It also helps control the costs of storing your data on Amazon S3.
L290: If you don't set a retention period, the Amazon S3 lifecycle configuration determines the duration that the objects are stored. The data retention policy that you've specified for the lifecycle configuration removes any query results that are older than the lifecycle configuration that you've specified. For more information, see cite29†Setting lifecycle configuration on a bucket .
L291: Data Wrangler uses Amazon S3 lifecycle configurations to manage data retention and expiration. You must give your Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic IAM execution role permissions to manage bucket lifecycle configurations. Use the following procedure to give permissions.
L292: 
L293: To give permissions to manage the lifecycle configuration do the following.
L294: 
L295:   1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console and open the IAM console at cite30†https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/†console.aws.amazon.com .
L296: 
L297:   2. Choose Roles.
L298:   3. In the search bar, specify the Amazon SageMaker AI execution role that Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic is using.
L299: 
L300:   4. Choose the role.
L301: 
L302:   5. Choose Add permissions.
L303: 
L304:   6. Choose Create inline policy.
L305: 
L306:   7. For Service, specify S3 and choose it.
L307: 
L308:   8. Under the Read section, choose GetLifecycleConfiguration.
L309: 
L310:   9. Under the Write section, choose PutLifecycleConfiguration.
L311: 
L312:   10. For Resources, choose Specific.
L313: 
L314:   11. For Actions, select the arrow icon next to Permissions management.
L315:   12. Choose PutResourcePolicy.
L316: 
L317:   13. For Resources, choose Specific.
L318: 
L319:   14. Choose the checkbox next to Any in this account.
L320: 
L321:   15. Choose Review policy.
L322: 
L323:   16. For Name, specify a name.
L324: 
L325:   17. Choose Create policy.
L326: ## Import data from Amazon Redshift
L327: 
L328: Amazon Redshift is a fully managed, petabyte-scale data warehouse service in the cloud. The first step to create a data warehouse is to launch a set of nodes, called an Amazon Redshift cluster. After you provision your cluster, you can upload your dataset and then perform data analysis queries.
L329: You can connect to and query one or more Amazon Redshift clusters in Data Wrangler. To use this import option, you must create at least one cluster in Amazon Redshift. To learn how, see cite31†Getting started with Amazon Redshift .
L330: 
L331: You can output the results of your Amazon Redshift query in one of the following locations:
L332: 
L333:   * The default Amazon S3 bucket
L334: 
L335:   * An Amazon S3 output location that you specify
L336: You can either import the entire dataset or sample a portion of it. For Amazon Redshift, it provides the following sampling options:
L337: 
L338:   * None – Import the entire dataset.
L339: 
L340:   * First K – Sample the first K rows of the dataset, where K is an integer that you specify.
L341: 
L342:   * Randomized – Takes a random sample of a size that you specify.
L343: 
L344:   * Stratified – Takes a stratified random sample. A stratified sample preserves the ratio of values in a column.
L345: The default Amazon S3 bucket is in the same AWS Region in which your Studio Classic instance is located to store Amazon Redshift query results. For more information, see cite9†Imported Data Storage .
L346: 
L347: For either the default Amazon S3 bucket or the bucket that you specify, you have the following encryption options:
L348: 
L349:   * The default AWS service-side encryption with an Amazon S3 managed key (SSE-S3)
L350: 
L351:   * An AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key that you specify
L352: An AWS KMS key is an encryption key that you create and manage. For more information on KMS keys, see cite32†AWS Key Management Service .
L353: 
L354: You can specify an AWS KMS key using either the key ARN or the ARN of your AWS account.
L355: 
L356: If you use the IAM managed policy, `AmazonSageMakerFullAccess`, to grant a role permission to use Data Wrangler in Studio Classic, your Database User name must have the prefix `sagemaker_access`.
L357: 
L358: Use the following procedures to learn how to add a new cluster.
L359: ###### Note
L360: 
L361: Data Wrangler uses the Amazon Redshift Data API with temporary credentials. To learn more about this API, refer to cite33†Using the Amazon Redshift Data API in the Amazon Redshift Management Guide.
L362: ###### To connect to a Amazon Redshift cluster
L363: 
L364:   1. Sign into cite25†Amazon SageMaker AI Console†console.aws.amazon.com .
L365: 
L366:   2. Choose Studio.
L367: 
L368:   3. Choose Launch app.
L369: 
L370:   4. From the dropdown list, select Studio.
L371: 
L372:   5. Choose the Home icon.
L373: 
L374:   6. Choose Data.
L375: 
L376:   7. Choose Data Wrangler.
L377: 
L378:   8. Choose Import data.
L379: 
L380:   9. Under Available, choose Amazon Athena.
L381: 
L382:   10. Choose Amazon Redshift.
L383: 
L384:   11. Choose Temporary credentials (IAM) for Type.
L385:   12. Enter a Connection Name. This is a name used by Data Wrangler to identify this connection.
L386: 
L387:   13. Enter the Cluster Identifier to specify to which cluster you want to connect. Note: Enter only the cluster identifier and not the full endpoint of the Amazon Redshift cluster.
L388: 
L389:   14. Enter the Database Name of the database to which you want to connect.
L390: 
L391:   15. Enter a Database User to identify the user you want to use to connect to the database.
L392:   16. For UNLOAD IAM Role, enter the IAM role ARN of the role that the Amazon Redshift cluster should assume to move and write data to Amazon S3. For more information about this role, see cite34†Authorizing Amazon Redshift to access other AWS services on your behalf in the Amazon Redshift Management Guide.
L393: 
L394:   17. Choose Connect.
L395: 
L396:   18. (Optional) For Amazon S3 output location, specify the S3 URI to store the query results.
L397:   19. (Optional) For KMS key ID, specify the ARN of the AWS KMS key or alias. The following image shows you where you can find either key in the AWS Management Console.
L398: 
L399: cite35†Image: The location of the AWS KMS alias ARN, alias name, and key ARN in the AWS KMS console. L400: 
L401: The following image shows all the fields from the preceding procedure.
L402: 
L403: cite36†Image: The Add Amazon Redshift connection panel. L404: After your connection is successfully established, it appears as a data source under Data Import. Select this data source to query your database and import data.
L405: ###### To query and import data from Amazon Redshift
L406: 
L407:   1. Select the connection that you want to query from Data Sources.
L408: 
L409:   2. Select a Schema. To learn more about Amazon Redshift Schemas, see cite37†Schemas in the Amazon Redshift Database Developer Guide.
L410: 
L411:   3. (Optional) Under Advanced configuration, specify the Sampling method that you'd like to use.
L412: 
L413:   4. Enter your query in the query editor and choose Run to run the query. After a successful query, you can preview your result under the editor.
L414:   5. Select Import dataset to import the dataset that has been queried.
L415: 
L416:   6. Enter a Dataset name. If you add a Dataset name that contains spaces, these spaces are replaced with underscores when your dataset is imported.
L417: 
L418:   7. Choose Add.
L419: 
L420: To edit a dataset, do the following.
L421: 
L422:   1. Navigate to your Data Wrangler flow.
L423: 
L424:   2. Choose the + next to Source - Sampled.
L425: 
L426:   3. Change the data that you're importing.
L427: 
L428:   4. Choose Apply
L429: ## Import data from Amazon EMR
L430: 
L431: You can use Amazon EMR as a data source for your Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler flow. Amazon EMR is a managed cluster platform that you can use process and analyze large amounts of data. For more information about Amazon EMR, see cite38†What is Amazon EMR? . To import a dataset from EMR, you connect to it and query it.
L432: 
L433: ###### Important
L434: 
L435: You must meet the following prerequisites to connect to an Amazon EMR cluster:
L436: ###### Prerequisites
L437: 
L438:   * ###### Network configurations
L439: 
L440:     * You have an Amazon VPC in the Region that you're using to launch Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic and Amazon EMR.
L441: 
L442:     * Both Amazon EMR and Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic must be launched in private subnets. They can be in the same subnet or in different ones.
L443: 
L444:     * Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic must be in VPC-only mode.
L445: 
L446: For more information about creating a VPC, see cite39†Create a VPC .
L447: For more information about creating a VPC, see cite40†Connect SageMaker Studio Classic Notebooks in a VPC to External Resources .
L448: 
L449:     * The Amazon EMR clusters that you're running must be in the same Amazon VPC.
L450: 
L451:     * The Amazon EMR clusters and the Amazon VPC must be in the same AWS account.
L452: 
L453:     * Your Amazon EMR clusters are running Hive or Presto.
L454: 
L455:       * Hive clusters must allow inbound traffic from Studio Classic security groups on port 10000.
L456:       * Presto clusters must allow inbound traffic from Studio Classic security groups on port 8889.
L457: ###### Note
L458: 
L459: The port number is different for Amazon EMR clusters using IAM roles. Navigate to the end of the prerequisites section for more information.
L460: 
L461:   * ###### SageMaker Studio Classic
L462: 
L463:     * Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic must run Jupyter Lab Version 3. For information about updating the Jupyter Lab Version, see cite41†View and update the JupyterLab version of an application from the console .
L464:     * Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic has an IAM role that controls user access. The default IAM role that you're using to run Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic doesn't have policies that can give you access to Amazon EMR clusters. You must attach the policy granting permissions to the IAM role. For more information, see cite42†Configure listing Amazon EMR clusters .
L465: 
L466:     * The IAM role must also have the following policy attached `secretsmanager:PutResourcePolicy`.
L467:     * If you're using a Studio Classic domain that you've already created, make sure that its `AppNetworkAccessType` is in VPC-only mode. For information about updating a domain to use VPC-only mode, see cite43†Shut Down and Update Amazon SageMaker Studio Classic .
L468: 
L469:   * ###### Amazon EMR clusters
L470: 
L471:     * You must have Hive or Presto installed on your cluster.
L472: 
L473:     * The Amazon EMR release must be version 5.5.0 or later.
L474: ###### Note

L233: ## cite79†Artificial Intelligence L234: # Pruning machine learning models with Amazon SageMaker Debugger and Amazon SageMaker Experiments
L235: 
L236: by Nathalie Rauschmayr, cite80†Julien Simon , and Satadal Bhattacharjee on 31 MAR 2020 in cite81†Amazon SageMaker , cite82†Artificial Intelligence cite83†Permalink cite84†Comments cite85†Share L237: In the past decade, deep learning has advanced many different areas, such as computer vision and natural language processing. State-of-the-art models now achieve near-human performance in tasks such as image classification. Deep neural networks can achieve this because they consist of millions of parameters that you train on large training datasets. For instance, the cite86†BERT (Large)†arxiv.org model consists of 340 million parameters, and cite87†Resnet-152†arxiv.org consists of 60 million parameters.
L238: Training such models from scratch is computationally intensive and can take hours, days, or even weeks.
L239: Typically, data scientists perform transfer learning, which is the process of using knowledge gained by solving one problem to a related but different problem. With transfer learning, you fine-tune a pretrained model on a smaller dataset to improve accuracy. In such scenarios, you may not need a large number of parameters in the model—a smaller model may just perform as well.
L240: In the context of machine learning (ML) at the edge, having small models is essential. Due to hardware constraints, factors such as latency, memory footprint, and compute time are as important as model accuracy. For instance, autonomous driving requires models with high accuracy and low latency. In such a scenario, a model that achieves 1% better accuracy but takes twice the time for prediction is not favorable.
L241: Model pruning can significantly reduce model size without sacrificing accuracy. The idea is simple: identify the redundant parameters in the model that contribute little to the training process.
L242: 
L243: This post demonstrates iterative model pruning with cite88†Amazon SageMaker . The post walks through a sample application that uses a pretrained model and iteratively prunes it by more than a factor of three with no significant loss in accuracy.
L244: ## Model pruning
L245: Model pruning aims to remove weights that don’t contribute much to the training process. Weights are learnable parameters: they are randomly initialized and optimized during the training process. During the forward pass, data passes through the model. The loss function evaluates model output given the labels; during the backward pass, weights are updated to minimize the loss. To do so, the gradients of the loss with respect to the weights are computed, and each weight receives a different update.
L246: After a few iterations, certain weights are typically more impactful than others; the goal of pruning is to remove the useless ones without significantly reducing model accuracy. The following diagram illustrates this workflow.
L247: cite89†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L248: 
L249: You can use the following heuristics to measure the importance of weights:
L250: 
L251:   * Magnitudes of weights – Remove weights if their absolute value is smaller than a threshold: smaller weights have less effect on the output.
L252:   * Average activation – If a neuron is mostly not active throughout the training, you can infer that the weights going into the activation function are less relevant.
L253: 
L254: You can distinguish between non-structured and structured weight pruning:
L255:   * Non-structured pruning removes arbitrary weights (as in the preceding diagram)
L256:   * Structured pruning removes entire convolutional filters and associated channels
L257: Structured pruning is especially relevant for computer vision models that typically consist of many convolutional layers. A filter is a collection of kernels (one kernel for every single input channel). A filter produces one feature map, also referred to as an output channel. The following diagram shows three kernels that produce three output feature maps.
L258: The number of parameters that the model has to learn (its weights) is 3 x input_channels x kernel_width x kernel_height, where the number of input channels in this example is 1. For simplification, you can assume in this diagram that there is no bias tensor. You can rank the filters to identify those of least importance (for instance, the yellow filter). You reduce the number of parameters by 1 x input_channels x kernel_width x kernel_height by removing it.
L259: cite90†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L260: To rank the importance of each filter, you employ the ranking method as described in the paper cite91†“Pruning Convolutional Neural Networks for Resource Efficient Inference”†arxiv.org : they estimate the impact of a pruned filter on the loss. The goal is to remove the ones that do not impact the loss. A filter receives a low rank if its activation outputs and corresponding gradients are small.
L261: You can get an estimate of filter importance by accumulating the product of activation outputs and gradients throughout the training.
L262: You then remove the lowest-ranked filters and fine-tune the model to recover from the pruning and regain accuracy. You can repeat these steps several times.
L263: ## Iterative model pruning on Amazon SageMaker
L264: cite92†Amazon SageMaker Debugger†docs.aws.amazon.com allows you to emit tensors from your training jobs and run built-in rules that automatically detect training issues. You can retrieve gradients and activation outputs to compute filter ranks. For more information, see cite93†Amazon SageMaker Debugger – Debug Your Machine Learning Models . Amazon SageMaker Experiments lets you customize, visualize, and track ML experiments at scale.
L265: For more information, see cite94†Amazon SageMaker Experiments – Organize, Track and Compare Your Machine Learning Trainings . For this post, you use it to track the different pruning iterations. You can quickly identify and deploy the model that yields the best accuracy and size trade-off with the Experiments view in Amazon SageMaker Studio.
L266: To walk through iterative model pruning step-by-step, this post uses a cite87†Resnet18†arxiv.org model pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tunes it on the cite95†Caltech101†www.vision.caltech.edu dataset, which consists of only 101 classes. You resize images during retraining. ResNet is a convolutional neural network consisting of multiple residual blocks. A block is made up of convolutional layers followed by a batch normalization layer and ReLu function. Skip connections allow the input to bypass the block.
L267: For this post, you use ResNet18, the smallest version of ResNet models with about 11 million parameters. In each pruning iteration, you remove the 200 lowest-ranked filters.
L268: The following diagram illustrates the solution workflow:
L269: 
L270: cite96†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L271: 
L272: The steps are as follows:
L273: 
L274:   1. Start the training job
L275:   2. Acquire the weights, gradients, biases, and activation outputs
L276:   3. Compute filter ranks
L277:   4. Prune low-ranking filters
L278:   5. Set new weights
L279:   6. Start the training job with the pruned model
L280: ## Creating the experiment and debugger hook configuration
L281: Before you implement the solution, create a model pruning experiment. An experiment is a collection of trials, whereby a trial is a collection of training steps. See the following code:
L282: 
L283:     `from smexperiments.experiment import Experiment
L284: 
L285:     Experiment.create(experiment_name="model_pruning_experiment",
L286:                         description="Iterative model pruning of ResNet18 trained on Caltech101",
L287:                         sagemaker_boto_client=sagemaker_boto_client)
L288:     `
L289: In each pruning iteration, you start a new Amazon SageMaker training job, which is a new trial within the experiment. See the following code:
L290: 
L291:     `from smexperiments.trial import Trial
L292: 
L293:     trial = Trial.create(experiment_name="model_pruning_experiment",
L294:     sagemaker_boto_client=sagemaker_boto_client)`
L295: You next define the `experiment_config`, which is a dictionary that is passed to the Amazon SageMaker training job. This allows Amazon SageMaker to associate the training job with the experiment and trial. See the following code:
L296: 
L297:     `experiment_config = { "ExperimentName": "model_pruning_experiment",
L298:                             "TrialName":  trial.trial_name,
L299:                             "TrialComponentDisplayName": "Training"}`
L300: Before you can start the training job, you must define a debugger hook configuration. Amazon SageMaker Debugger provides default collections for weights, biases, gradients, and losses . For this post, you must also store  activation outputs. To retrieve those, create a custom collection in which a regular expression indicates the tensor names to include. Because ResNet consists of batch norm layers, you also store the batch norm statistics running mean and variance.
L301: Tensors are saved every 100 steps, wherein a step presents one forward and backward pass. See the following code:
L302: 
L303:     `from sagemaker.debugger import DebuggerHookConfig, CollectionConfig
L304: 
L305:     debugger_hook_config = DebuggerHookConfig(
L306:           collection_configs=[
L307:               CollectionConfig(
L308:                     name="custom_collection",
L309:                     parameters={ "include_regex": ".*relu|.*weight|.*bias|.*running_mean|.*running_var",
L310:                                  "save_interval": "100" })])`
L311: ## Starting your training job
L312: You are now ready to train the ResNet18 model with Amazon SageMaker. The training loop is defined in the `entry_point` file `train.py`. For more information, see the cite97†GitHub repo†github.com . To emit tensors, pass the debugger hook configuration into the PyTorch Estimator. See the following code:
L313: 
L314:     `import sagemaker
L315:     from sagemaker.pytorch import PyTorch
L316: 
L317:     estimator = PyTorch(role=sagemaker.get_execution_role(),
L318:                       train_instance_count=1,
L319:                       train_instance_type='ml.p3.2xlarge',
L320:                       train_volume_size=400,
L321:                       source_dir='src',
L322:                       entry_point='train.py',
L323:                       framework_version='1.3.1',
L324:                       py_version='py3',
L325:                       debugger_hook_config=debugger_hook_config
L326:             )
L327:     `
L328: After you define the estimator object, you can call `fit`. This launches a managed ml.p3.2xlarge instance to run your training script. As discussed previously, you pass the `experiment_config` to the training job. See the following code:
L329: 
L330:     `estimator.fit(experiment_config=experiment_config)`
L331: ## Getting gradients, weights, and biases
L332: After the training job is complete, you retrieve its tensors, such as gradients, weights, and biases. You can use the cite98†smdebug†pypi.org library, which provides functions to read and filter tensors. First, create a cite99†trial†github.com that allows access to the tensors that the debugger saved. For more information, see the cite99†GitHub repo†github.com . In the context of Amazon SageMaker Debugger, a trial is an object that lets you query tensors for a given training job.
L333: In the context of Amazon SageMaker Experiments, a trial is part of an experiment and presents a collection of training steps involved in a single training job. See the following code:
L334: 
L335:     `from smdebug.trials import create_trial
L336: 
L337:     path = estimator.latest_job_debugger_artifacts_path()
L338:     smdebug_trial = create_trial(path)`
L339: To access tensor values, call `smdebug_trial.tensor()`. For instance, to get the activation outputs of the first convolution layer, enter the following code:
L340: 
L341:     `smdebug_trial.tensor('layer1.0.relu_0_output_0').value(0, mode=modes.TRAIN)`
L342: ## Computing filter ranks
L343: Now that you have access to the tensors, you can compute their filter ranks. Iterate the available training steps and retrieve the activation outputs and their gradients. For instance, the following code segment computes the filter ranks of the first feature layer of the model, and you then compute a single value (rank) for each filter:
L344: 
L345:     `rank = 0
L346:     for step in smdebug_trial.steps(mode=modes.TRAIN):
L347:         activation_output = smdebug_trial.tensor( 'layer1.0.relu_0_output_0').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L348:         gradient = smdebug_trial.tensor( 'gradient/layer1.0.relu_ReLU_output').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L349:         product = activation_output * gradient
L350:         rank += np.mean(product, axis=(0,2,3))`
L351: Afterwards, you normalize filter ranks and sort them by size.
L352: ## Pruning low-ranking filters
L353: 
L354: You can now retrieve the smallest filters. The following code shows that you can prune filter 1, 36, and 127 in `layer1.0` because they have a rank of 0.0:
L355: 
L356:     `[('layer1.0.relu_ReLU_output', 1, 0.0),
L357:     ('layer1.0.relu_ReLU_output', 127, 0.0),
L358:     ('layer1.0.relu_ReLU_output', 36, 0.0)]`
L359: To prune those filters, use SageMaker Debugger to get the weight tensor of the first convolutional layer in `layer1.0` and delete the preceding entries in the second dimension (`axis=1`). See the following code:
L360: 
L361:     `weight = trial.tensor('ResNet_layer1.0.conv1.weight').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L362:     weight = np.delete(weight, [1,36,127], axis=1)`
L363: ## Setting new weights
L364: You also need to adjust the convolution parameters. The convolutional layer in `layer1.0` in the Resnet18 model has 64 output channels. After removing three filters, it only has 61 output channels. You also need to adjust the weights of the subsequent batch norm layer. Therefore, remove the entries in the first dimension (`axis=0`). See the following code:
L365: 
L366:     `weight = trial.tensor('ResNet_layer1.0.bn1.weight').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L367:     bias = trial.tensor('ResNet_layer1.0.bn1.bias').value(step, mode=modes.TRAIN)
L368:     weight = np.delete(weight, [1,36,127], axis=0)
L369:     bias =  np.delete(bias, [1,36,127], axis=0)`
L370: ## Starting the next pruning iteration
L371: 
L372: After you prune the 200 smallest filters, save the new model definition with the latest weights and start the next pruning iteration. You can complete these steps multiple times, which leads to a smaller model in each iteration.
L373: ## Results
L374: You can track and visualize the iterative model pruning experiment in Amazon SageMaker Studio. The training script uses SageMaker Debugger’s `save_scalar` method to store the number of model parameters and model accuracy. For more information, see the cite100†GitHub repo†github.com . The values that `save_scalar` writes go into a data store that Amazon SageMaker Studio uses to create visualizations.
L375: The following graph shows a scatterplot in which the x-axis shows the number of model parameters and the y-axis shows the validation accuracy.
L376: cite101†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L377: 
L378: Initially, the model consisted of 11 million parameters. After 11 iterations, the number of parameters reduced to 706,000, and accuracy increased to 90% and started dropping after eight pruning iterations. The following screenshot shows the experiment view where the different trials and details are listed.
L379: 
L380: cite102†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L381: ## Running iterative model pruning with a custom rule
L382: In the previous example, accuracy drops when the model has fewer than 4 million parameters. You want to stop the experiment when you reach this point. SageMaker Debugger provides built-in rules that trigger when the model training runs into issues, such as for instance vanishing gradients or the loss is not decreasing. If the model does not have enough capacity (too few parameters), it doesn’t learn well. One of the implications is that the loss may not decrease.
L383: For more information, see cite103†Built-in Rules Provided by Amazon SageMaker Debugger†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L384: For this post, you can define a custom rule that compares the accuracy of the current model with the accuracy of the previous training job. For example, if it drops by more than 10%, the rule triggers and returns `True`. You can then set up an cite104†Amazon CloudWatch alarm and cite105†AWS Lambda function that stops the training job and prevents your model pruning experiment from wasting resources on jobs that produce low-quality models. For more information, see the cite106†GitHub repo†github.com .
L385: The following code shows a high-level overview of the custom rule:
L386: 
L387:     `from smdebug.rules.rule import Rule
L388: 
L389:     class check_accuracy(Rule):
L390:         def __init__(self, base_trial,
L391:                      previous_accuracy=0.0):
L392:               self.previous_accuracy = float(previous_accuracy)
L393: 
L394:         def invoke_at_step(self, step):
L395:             predictions = np.argmax(self.base_trial.tensor('CrossEntropyLoss_0_input_0').value(step, mode=modes.EVAL), axis=1)
L396:             labels = self.base_trial.tensor('CrossEntropyLoss_0_input_1').value(step, mode=modes.EVAL)
L397:             current_accuracy = compute_accurcay(predictions, labels)
L398: 
L399:             if self.previous_accuracy - current_accuracy > 0.10:
L400:                 return True
L401: 
L402:              return False
L403:     `
L404: The rule implements a Python class that inherits from the `smdebug` rule class. It takes as argument the accuracy of the previous training job. The class implements the function `invoke_at_step` that is called every time tensors of a new step are available. With `smdebug`, you get the inputs into the loss function, which are the model predictions and labels. You can then compute the accuracy and compare it to the previous training job.
L405: For more information about the full implementation of the rule, see the cite107†GitHub repo†github.com .
L406: To run the rule with your training job, you need to pass it to the PyTorch estimator object. You first need to create a custom rule configuration. See the following code:
L407: 
L408:     `from sagemaker.debugger import Rule, CollectionConfig, rule_configs
L409: 
L410:     check_accuracy_rule = Rule.custom(
L411:         name='CheckAccuracy',
L412:         image_uri='840043622174.dkr.ecr.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sagemaker-debugger-rule-evaluator:latest',
L413:         instance_type='ml.c4.xlarge',
L414:         volume_size_in_gb=400,
L415:         source='custom_rule/check_accuracy.py',
L416:         rule_to_invoke='check_accuracy',
L417:         rule_parameters={"previous_accuracy": "0.0"},
L418:     )
L419:     `
L420: The rule configuration specifies the location of the rule definition, its input parameters, and the instance type where the rule container is going to run. You need to specify the image for the rule container. For more information, see cite108†Amazon SageMaker Custom Rule Evaluator Registry Ids†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L421: 
L422: After you define the rule, pass the argument `rules = [check_accuracy_rule]` to the Pytorch estimator.
L423: In each pruning iteration, you need to pass the accuracy of the previous training job to the rule, which is retrievable via SageMaker Experiments and the `ExperimentAnalytics` module. See the following code:
L424: 
L425:     `from sagemaker.analytics import ExperimentAnalytics
L426: 
L427:     trial_component_analytics = ExperimentAnalytics(experiment_name="model_pruning_experiment")
L428:     accuracy = trial_component_analytics.dataframe()['scalar/accuracy_EVAL - Max'][0]
L429:     `
L430: Overwrite the value in the rule configuration with the following code:
L431: 
L432:     `check_accuracy_rule.rule_parameters["previous_accuracy"] = str(accuracy)`
L433: In each iteration, check the job status. If the previous job stops, exit the loop. See the following code:
L434: 
L435:     `job_name = estimator.latest_training_job.name
L436:     client = estimator.sagemaker_session.sagemaker_client
L437:     description = client.describe_training_job(TrainingJobName=job_name)
L438:     if description['TrainingJobStatus'] == 'Stopped':
L439:         break
L440:     `
L441: The following graph shows the number of parameters versus accuracy. In contrast to the previous experiment, the training job stops when it produces a low-quality model, and the experiment ends. As a consequence, it only runs eight iterations.
L442: 
L443: cite109†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L444: 
L445: The following screenshot shows the Debugger view in SageMaker Studio. It shows that the custom rule found an issue.
L446: 
L447: cite110†Image†d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net L448: For more information about defining and running custom rules with SageMaker Debugger, see cite111†How to Use Custom Rules†docs.aws.amazon.com .
L449: ## Conclusion
L450: 
L451: This post discussed iterative model pruning with Amazon SageMaker and how you can significantly reduce the size of your models and retain accuracy by identifying redundant parameters that contribute little to the training process. You walked through a sample application that uses a pretrained model and saw that the model did not lose accuracy when iteratively pruned.
